speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF LATE J.S. WOODSWORTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to notice which I gave to Your Honour this morning, and as a matter of privilege, I should like to draw the attention of the House to the significance of this day in Canada's history. It was on December 6, 1921, exactly 50 years ago today, that the late J. S. Woodsworth was first elected to the Parliament of Canada. We in this party are of course deeply conscious of our debt to him for what he did for our movement. I think it might also be said that few men have made a mark on the history of this country such as that made by the former member for Winnipeg North Centre, whom I had the honour to succeed when he died in 1942.
I believe members of the House might be interested in knowing that his widow, Mrs. Lucy Woodsworth, now 97 years of age, is resident in Ottawa at St. Vincent hospital. It may well be that members would like our greetings to be extended to her on this occasion. If so, I know of no one more qualified to do that than the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Woodsworth, the distinguished member for Van-couver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis).

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON OUTBREAK OF WAR BETWEEN INDIA AND PAKISTAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know that I speak for all members of the House when I express the government's profound regret that open war has broken out on the subcontinent of India.
General hostilities erupted between India and Pakistan last Friday. Each government has accused the other of having started this latest stage in their tense confrontation which began some eight months ago. Reports of the fighting are contradictory. It seems fairly clear that neither side has yet heavily committed its forces on the western front; in and around East Pakistan, however, Indian forces are exerting considerable efforts to gain territory. India has recognized the provisonal government of Bangla Desh.
An emergency session of the United Nations Security Council was called Saturday evening on the initiative of nine of its members to consider the deteriorating situation. It met again on Sunday and will meet also this afternoon. A number of resolutions have been presented but no consensus is yet in sight. Our ambassador at the United Nations is in close touch with events there and is keeping us informed. It is our hope that the Security Council will find enough common ground to be able to act decisively. In the absence of such action, it will be necessary to consider what the General Assembly could achieve.
The safety of Canadian citizens on the subcontinent has been very much in our minds this weekend. In India, there are some 1,100 Canadians registered with the High Commission in Delhi. More than a month ago, those living near the border with Pakistan were advised to consider moving to a safer location. In East Pakistan there are 40. In the early hours of this morning, at the request of the Secretary General of the United Nations, a Canadian Armed Forces C-130 aircraft was diverted to Dacca to help in the evacuation of United Nations personnel. It was intended that it should also be available to any Canadians who might not have left earlier, Commonwealth citizens and other nationals. Although a local ceasefire had been arranged by the United Nations with the Pakistani, Indian and Mukti Bahini forces which would permit the aircraft to land at Dacca, that airport was attacked at precisely the hour our aircraft was to begin its approach to the area. The aircraft returned to Bangkok safely. We trust that with renewed assurances of another local ceasefire, we shall have better success tomorrow.
In West Pakistan, where 270 Canadians are registered at the High Commission in Islamabad, those responsible on the spot have not yet concluded that action is necessary. Some time ago Canadians in the Lahore area were advised to consider moving, and it was suggested to those in Karachi that they should be prepared to leave at short notice. Yesterday nine Canadians arrived in Teheran on a commercial flight from Karachi; their families have been informed. There have been reports that other commercial flights have followed.
From the beginning Canada has been in touch with the governments of India and Pakistan at the highest levels. To the government of India we have urged patience and restraint in a situation of great difficulty. To the government of Pakistan we have stressed the urgent necessity of speeding up of a return to civilian and representative government, particularly in East Pakistan. We have been among the most concerned and engaged in the great world humanitarian effort to succor the refugees, and have latterly been directing our efforts to increased assistance to India to help relieve the burden on its budget and

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON OUTBREAK OF WAR BETWEEN INDIA AND PAKISTAN
speechtext:
It is needless to say, Mr. Speaker, that it was with heavy heart that I listened to the minister's statement. I know that I share with him and all hon. members a profound sense of sorrow at the developments which we have been learning about in recent days and hours in the Indian subcontinent.
We are, of course, particularly concerned about the welfare, safety and security of our own nationals in the area. I am particularly distressed that certain hostile actions have been taken at times, not only in the place mentioned by the minister but at other evacuation points, when the innocent and proper removal of civilians was being undertaken. It is deplorable and regrettable. I hope we will not have further reports of such unfortunate incidents.
The whole question in recent months has not brought forth much reason for optimism. For a long time we should all have seen the gathering clouds over the Indian subcontinent, and should have been prepared for the prospects of the kind of warfare which is being waged by these two countries at the present time. For months there has been tragedy in the subcontinent. Now, with the opening of hostilities, the tragedy has been widened and broadened and given more painful dimensions, and who knows how horrendous might be the situation if this continues.
It is all the more painful, I think, because these are friendly states of the Commonwealth. We feared the situation and we wondered. The burden which India had to bear was a terribly heavy one. Yet, while neither a pacifist nor a dove, I can never believe that a warlike solution today is in fact a solution to problems of this kind. Perhaps the world has not taken sufficient note of the dimensions of the problem. Perhaps the international community should have moved more quickly. Now it is too late to pass judgment on the past.
I am sure everyone here is disturbed about the seeming incapacity so far of the Security Council to take effective action, indeed, Sir, to take any action on this terrible, awful conflict involving so many people and with the grim potentiality of involving so many more. The Security Council, having met hour after hour, seems to end with the use of the veto and in futility. Whether it will be necessary to move from the Security Council to the General Assembly through the technique of the "uniting for peace resolution", as it was once called, we do not know. I would hope the minister might tell us more about the Canadian government's point of view on that. I hope he will also be able to tell us more about what the Canadian nation and the Canadian delegation are prepared to do.
I thank him for this statement. I realize there is not much he can say at this time, but I hope that in the future he will keep the House and the country informed. I can assure him that all of my colleagues, and I am sure all Canadians of decent outlook and concern for the peace of the world, will support the Canadian government in any measure which it can take to help roll back the frontiers of hatred and bring about as quickly as possible that which surely is of the essence today, the cessation of hostilities through a ceasefire.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON OUTBREAK OF WAR BETWEEN INDIA AND PAKISTAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is unnecessary to assure the Secretary of State for External Affairs that we appreciate the efforts the government has obviously taken to assure the safety of Canadian nationals in the area referred to. It is also unnecessary, I think, to say to him that we appreciate fully the difficulties of the situation and the fact that the contribution which Canada is able to make in the solution of the political and military problem is necessarily limited.
I want to underline in my comments on the minister's statement the seriousness of the war not only for the people directly concerned, the people of India and Pakistan and the people of East Pakistan, but for the future peace of the world. The failure of the Security Council to arrive at any consensus, Mr. Speaker, is not accidental; it is due to the fact that the Soviet Union has launched itself on one side and Mainland China has launched itself on the opposite side and the United States of America is trying to make up its mind precisely where it belongs. It is the ranging on opposite sides by these big powers that makes it impossible for the Security Council to reach any solution to the problem and makes the war so dangerous to the future peace of the world.
I say through you, Mr. Speaker-and I hope not presumptuously to the people concerned on this subcontinent-that if the war continues very long and attracts the forces of perhaps China on one side and the Soviet Union on the other, or accelerated military assistance from one side or the other or both, then obviously world war will come a step closer and the danger of nuclear destruction will become as serious as it has ever been since the end of the last war. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, without wanting to be dramatic about the subject I think the Canadian government ought to consider very seriously whether the matter should be left very much longer with the Security Council in view of the futility which has resulted from that or whether it should be taken to the General Assembly where the veto does not exist and perhaps the international world might take some steps to advance peace in the area.
I think it is important to remember that this outbreak of war is the result of many years of conflict and was particularly sharpened by the shortsightedness of American policy in 1958 or so when the Indian declaration of nonalignment suggested to Mr. Dulles and his associates in Washington that Pakistan ought to be militarily strengthened. It ought also to be remembered that the war has occurred because of the completely indefensible step taken by Mr. Yahya Khan, the head of the government in West Pakistan, against the Awami League, which had won all of the seats in East Pakistan and some in West Pakistan in a democratic election in that country. Mr. Yahya had refused to permit Sheik Mujib to become the head of government of all Pakistan as the election required him to do. Instead, he has imposed a military government and has outlawed the Awami League and imprisoned not only Sheik Mujib but others as well. In our anxiety to have the war ended by a ceasefire-all members of my party in the House are as anxious to see that as any other member or any other citizen of Canada-we should not fail to remember what Yahya Khan has done to the democratic process in Pakistan and to the people of East Pakistan and no step

should be taken at the expense of the freedom and the future of the people of East Pakistan.
May I also say a word which I imagine is unnecessary but which I feel ought to be put on record. This war ought in no way to interfere with the assistance given, and which must be continued, to India to deal with the eight to ten million East Pakistani refugees now in India who require succour and aid. I am sure the Secretary of State for External Affairs will agree that Canada will in no way reduce its determination to continue its assistance to the refugees, and I hope our influence will be used so that other countries in the world will not cease or reduce their aid.
All of us in this House hope that some solution may be found to this war, perhaps a temporary ceasefire to be followed by a political solution that will recognize the rights and the freedom of the people of East Pakistan and, indeed, of West Pakistan as well, and that the military junta, to use a South American term for an Asiatic government, that now seeks to control all Pakistan will be dispossessed of its power by the free democratic process of the Pakistani people.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON OUTBREAK OF WAR BETWEEN INDIA AND PAKISTAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we were aghast at hearing, over the past few days, the news concerning the war between India and Pakistan. I believe few Canadians have any hope of immediate settlement of that war, at least so long as the issue remains in the hands of the Security Council.
Last night again, I was listening to news on television coming to us from New York, where the aristocracy of the world boldly plays politics on the occasion of such serious conflicts as the one opposing India and Pakistan. So long as powers like Communist China and Russia will be providing the two parties involved with arms, there is little hope that peace may be restored in that part of the world. Furthermore, so long as wars will supply major markets for arms manufacturers, notwithstanding the United States, embargo on shipments of arms to India, nations will lie at the mercy of warfaring countries. It is an open secret, Mr. Speaker, that major international arms manufacturers need no permission for their arms.
I believe the government and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) share our pessimism judging by the very important security measures that have been taken in order to ensure the evacuation of Canadians living in that part of the world.
Mr. Speaker, when such conflicts arise we should let the countries concerned, in this case Pakistan, settle them. The world would then be better off.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: INDIA-PAKISTAN WAR-POSSIBLE CONSIDERATION BY UNITED NATIONS GENERAL ASSEMBLY-COMMONWEALTH ACTION TO ACHIEVE CEASEFIRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I was in Washington on Friday this was one of the subjects I discussed with the Secretary of State of the United States. That was before the discussion had begun. He laid before me his view that what was important now was a ceasefire. As the hon. members know, so far his efforts to get agreement on that have been aborted. Many other efforts have been made. While I am pessimistic, as I think anyone must be, I for one have not yet reached the point where I would want the Security Council to throw in the sponge. I repeat that a discussion in the United Nations General Assembly is not the same as getting an agreed resolution from the Security Council. To have a general discussion in the

United Nations, as we know from many previous occasions, is more likely to exacerbate than resolve the difficulties.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: INDIA-PAKISTAN WAR-POSSIBLE CONSIDERATION BY UNITED NATIONS GENERAL ASSEMBLY-COMMONWEALTH ACTION TO ACHIEVE CEASEFIRE
speechtext: Has any effort been made within the Commonwealth to formulate a concerted approach to bring about pressure for a ceasefire?

subsubtopic: INDIA-PAKISTAN WAR-POSSIBLE CONSIDERATION BY UNITED NATIONS GENERAL ASSEMBLY-COMMONWEALTH ACTION TO ACHIEVE CEASEFIRE
speechtext: Before hostilities broke out, Mr. Speaker, several efforts were made by various members of the Commonwealth to offer their good offices but they were rejected. I do not think the prospects now are as good as they were then. In my view, efforts within the Commonwealth are likely to be met with very great difficulty. At the moment, I do not think either side is disposed to do anything but continue the hostilities that unfortunately have begun.

speechtext: My supplementary arises out of the last question asked by the Leader of the Opposition. Would the minister consider doing this, because certainly we have a large volume of good will in those countries and no one could suggest we have any interest there other than an interest in world peace?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to revert to a point of order that has arisen in connection with Bill C-259. This bill has been fraught with difficulties from the very day of its inception. You may recall that when I first spoke on this bill on second reading there had to be prepared a curative motion because of the difficulty that arose in that Bill C-259 departed in major ways from the ways and means motion that had been adopted by the House.
What concerns me now is that we have some 150 or more amendments before the House, and there is a question as to whether any of them are valid. I would put this matter to Your Honour for consideration because I think it is very urgent. There is no question that the point of order is hypothetical or anticipatory because amendments have been adopted by the committee, and again I would put it to you that there may be a question as to their validity.
I am concerned primarily with the special order on the bill which was adopted by the House on September 28. You will recall that after some difficulty, after the motion had been made and Your Honour had given it a good deal of thought, you did make a ruling on it, because I had pointed out that Bill C-259 differed from the ways and means motion and therefore was not properly before the House. I further raised the question-even when the hurdles were overcome-since the ways and means motion was in the form of a bill whether a committee or any member thereof could amend or reject any provision of a

December 6, 1971
Inquiries of the Ministry
bill based upon the ways and means motion, since any such amendment or rejection would vary a question already decided upon by the House in June following on the adoption of the general budgetary resolutions. Those amendments would therefore be out of order.
May I refer to what Your Honour said at that time, and I quote:
If the House of Commons accepts this procedure and adopts as part of the ways and means resolution a draft bill, I do not see how any amendment can be adopted or suggested to the House at any time thereafter either by the government or the opposition, because the objection can be very well made at any time an amendment is made by the government, the opposition, a member of the opposition or any individual member of the House that this amendment is not in keeping or in accordance with the terms of the ways and means resolution. It will not be, of course, because it is different from the draft bill which has been submitted.
I think the House got itself into a bit of a bind and difficulty by following this procedure. I think it should be for the House to find a way out of it. For the moment, I suggest to hon. members that we proceed with the bill before us.
Then, Your Honour suggested that perhaps the House leaders should meet and find a solution. That excerpt is from Hansard of September 13, 1971. On September 28, at about five minutes to six, the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council put the following motion to the House:
That, notwithstanding the terms of the ways and means motion upon which Bill C-259 was introduced, this House deems that the said bill was properly introduced within the terms of Standing Order 60, provided that the form of the said ways and means motion shall not be accepted as a precedent in any future case;
That appears at page 8249 of Hansard. I have no quarrel with the first paragraph; the second paragraph is the one that is deficient. It reads as follows:
And that it shall be an instruction to the committee of the whole on the said bill that the admissibility of any proposed amendments thereto shall be governed by the bill as read a second time, and shall not be limited by the said ways and means motion although all other procedures relating to financial or tax measures shall apply.
I refer primarily to the mandatory nature of those two paragraphs. I point out to Your Honour that Nay's Parliamentary Practice, 17th edition, at page 536 contains the following statement:
Before the committee, to which a bill has been committed, commences its consideration of the bill, an instruction may be given to such committee, the purpose of which is either to empower the committee to do something which it could not otherwise do, or to define the course of action which it must follow. The first type of instruction is called permissive, the second mandatory.
Instructions may be given not only to a committee of the whole House, but to any other committee. An instruction to a committee of the whole House can only be moved in the permissive form.-
That is why I say that the word "shall" cannot appear in that particular motion made by the parliamentary secretary. The reason I am raising this particular point is that I think we can cure it but it must be posted in the same way Your Honour posted the flag on the procedure that was used in June with regard to the bill. This type of operation must not be repeated, and I am suggesting that what has been done on this occasion must not be repeated. In effect the instruction to the committee on Bill C-259 is that the committee must, with regard to the admissibility of

amendments, follow the substance of the bill and ignore the ways and means resolution. There is no doubt that the instruction is mandatory and should be declared out of order.
Further, a second rule applying to instructions to a committee of the whole is that the instruction is invalid if its effect would be to widen the powers of the committee beyond the ways and means resolution which governs the bill. I refer again to May's 17th edition at page 541, where we consider instructions to the committee. I shall not quote the whole of subparagraph 5 which indicates that you cannot extend the powers of the committee. I do not want to go further on that particular point.
The third point to which I wish to direct Your Honour's attention is contained in Redlich, "The Procedure of the House of Commons", Volume II, at page 197. The instruction to the committee was not made an order of the day; it was merely a motion which stayed under "motions" and it is a fact the chairman of the committee did not incorporate into the record of the proceedings of the committee the direction from the House, even though the direction from the House may be deficient on other points. It was not done in the committee. All I am pointing out is what should be done properly. The motion of the parliamentary secretary should have been made an order of the day so that it would have been referred directly to the chairman and then he would have read it in committee.
I know this is a long, difficult point of order, and that it is perhaps a refinement, so to that extent I apologize to the House. But having raised the first point of order on second reading which clarified the procedures, Mr. Speaker, I thought that again it was incumbent to do it at this time. After all, the minister is going to come forward at some time with other changes in the Income Tax Act following the type of mini-budget of October 14, again for a first time practice, so I think it is incumbent that we have correct procedures and guidelines with regard to these new rules. Now is the time to straighten this out, although it appears to be rather nitpicking, so that in future we can be guided by what Your Honour has said on the previous point and, I would submit, on consideration of what I have raised this afternoon when Your Honour is ready to indicate again the guidelines for the future conduct of the House within the meaning of Standing Order 60.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
What I shall do is this. I shall outline as clearly as I can the content of the amendments and then, after that, if we think something else is necessary, we can decide what course to take.
Last week I announced that the government would introduce relieving amendments for co-operatives, credit unions and caisses populaires. I would now like to explain the nature of these amendments in more detail. I shall deal first with co-operatives.
Under the present act, the patronage dividends of a co-operative could not reduce its income below 3 per cent of capital employed. With the introduction of Bill C-259 an attempt was made to re-examine the appropriate tax treatment of co-operatives. Bill C-259, and the several amendments to C-259 which the government has previously moved, reflect a new percentage limit, a new definition of capital employed and other transitional and long term rules designed to establish an appropriate level of taxation for co-operatives.
During this period, the government has continued to communicate with the co-operative movement. Representatives of that industry and many members on both sides of this House have argued persuasively that the "capital employed" concept is inappropriate in the case of the
December 6, 1971
Income Tax Act
co-operatives and that, with the introduction of general tax reform, a new and better system should be developed. Rather than modifying the old system-a system which was inappropriate to start with-the government was urged to seek a new and more appropriate method which would recognize that a co-operative is a group of people who have organized to help themselves.
The government has decided to abandon the notion of "capital employed" and henceforth co-operatives will no longer be taxed on income from business with members which is distributed to members in the form of patronage dividends.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Therefore, the limit on deductibility of patronage dividends will be removed. In its place, the government proposes that there be a withholding tax at the rate of 15 per cent on patronage dividends in excess of $100 paid to a member in any year. The withholding tax would, of course, be refundable to the extent it exceeded a taxpayer's tax liability.
This new approach will have the following results. Recipients of patronage dividends will be treated as before: if the patronage dividend relates to the recipient's business it will be included in his income for tax purposes. In other circumstances, it will not be taxed. The withholding of tax by the co-operative will permit the government to administer the system efficiently and yet obtain the appropriate result depending on the character of the patronage dividend in the hands of the recipient. This change will provide substantial relief to co-operatives concerned about their treatment under the new Act.
I should like now to deal with Credit Unions and Caisses Populaires. The main concern expressed by credit unions and caisses populaires involves the reserves they must set aside under provincial statutes. It has been pointed out that these mandatory reserves exceed the reserves allowed against income for tax purposes, and that they are unlike the ordinary surplus of a corporation in that they cannot be distributed to members. Credit unions and caisses populaires argued that they could not obtain the same enjoyment of the small business deductions as other corporations which were not subject to provincial regulations. As a result, small credit unions and caisses populaires felt subject to the high rate of corporate tax prematurely.
In response to this argument, the government will introduce an amendment the effect of which will be to tax the income of a credit union or caisse populaire at the rate of 25 per cent as long as the reserves in excess of those allowed against income do not exceed 5 per cent of deposits and share capital. This will be accomplised by an adjustment of the small business deduction. As I understand it from my discussions, this amendment will provide the last remaining goal sought by the credit union movement.
This special right to use an effective corporate tax rate of 25 per cent might not in itself be sufficient for small credit unions or caisses populaires which would need a reserve in excess of 5 per cent of financial stability. Accordingly, the small business deduction available to other corporations will continue to apply so that a credit

union or caisse populaire can build up $300,000 of reserves out of income taxed at 25 per cent whether or not such reserves exceed 5 per cent of deposits and share capital.
The right to build up 5 per cent reserves will, of course, only apply to increases in those reserves after 1971. Transitionally, the credit union or caisse populaire will be considered to have reserves equal to the lesser of the maximum 5 per cent of deposits and share capital or the actual reserves measured by taking assets at their value for tax purposes. Thus, if the actual opening reserves are less than 5 per cent they may be built up to 5 per cent out of income taxed at 25 per cent in the future. If the actual opening reserves are greater than 5 per cent, the fact that such extra reserves have been accumulated in the past will not affect the right of the credit union to use a 25 per cent rate in the future. The government believes that in this way credit unions and caisses populaires will be able to obtain the appropriate entitlement to the small business deduction and thereby enjoy the benefit of a 25 per cent rate of tax on an appropriate amount of income.
Finally, as a consequence of abandoning the notion of capital employed for co-operatives, the government does not believe it to be appropriate to retain this concept for credit unions and caisses populaires. Therefore, the government proposes that the limit on interest rebates related to capital employed be deleted. This is something they did not ask for. They are getting it as a throw-away.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Chairman, this amendment is very close to the one I suggested. If I am not mistaken I have a formal amendment before the committee on this matter, and when it comes to the point of the question being put I am prepared to withdraw my amendment in favour of the one that the government has put forward.
In large part, the amendment now before us meets the objection I raised. The fundamental problem here is that if the minister made no decision on an application for registration of a charitable organization, or of some other organization, there would be no ground for appeal because an appeal could only arise as the result of a
[Mr. MacEachen.)
refusal. In this particular case, the applicant would be completely frustrated in his desire to come to a decision. My suggestion was that a time limit should be imposed during which the minister must make a decision, and if he did not he would be deemed to have refused the application so that an appeal could be allowed. In large part the proposed amendment covers this point.
The only point I should like to raise, and my colleague from Edmonton West raised it when we discussed the section earlier, is that sometimes when an outside limit is established it becomes the accepted norm in the department. The officials feel they have six months to consider the application and do not concern themselves with it until the six months have passed. I sincerely hope that the effect of this amendment will not be for the departmental officials to consider that they have six months in which to consider the application. I hope that the parliamentary secretary can assure the committee that the maximum time within which the minister must reply will not become the minimum time. Aside from that general principle, and subject to certain comments which my colleague from Edmonton West may have, the amendment generally meets the proposal I made.

The Minister of the Environment may call it sedentary, but he may improve his knowledge of the income tax laws by sitting here. This is the only way cabinet members will be able to do it, because they certainly did not know what was in it before. Why should the person in British Columbia, Newfoundland or some other point to which it may take between three and five days to send a letter be penalized, whereas the person in Toronto, Montreal, Ottawa or other point close to the capital have an advantage because he gets his mail delivered quickly. I point out to the officials concerned that mail leaving Ottawa on Wednesday, and very definitely mail going out on Thursday, very often is not delivered in certain areas until Tuesday morning.
That happens in Hull.

I am told that this happens in Hull. I give the benefit of reasonable doubt, shall we say, to the post office with regard to reasonable performance. The parliamentary secretary knows that these delays occur in Calgary. Mail which arrives in Calgary on Friday afternoon will not be delivered on Saturday or Sunday. Because of the accumulation of mail in the post office, it will not be sorted and delivered on Monday. One must wait until Tuesday. What on earth prevents notice beginning from the date of receipt of that notice by the recipient? What prevents that? Would that not bring justice in this regard right across the country?
You know, Mr. Chairman, I have often complained in the past about what I call the capital city syndrome which applies to people who sit in comfortable pews. They only worry for two or three days about the delivery of letters and then they can go to their lawyers. They have the time to do it. Do not let anyone say to me or to any member representing one of the farther reaches of the country, "A person can go to a judge and get leave to open the case." Do you know just how much it costs to do that? Such suggestions are even worse than Marie Antoinette saying, "If they cannot get bread, let them eat cake." I defy anyone to make an application to a judge, either of the federal court or of the Supreme Court, for less than $250. That is the cost of such an ex parte application. One has to retain an Ottawa representative, and there must be an appearance at the Supreme Court or at the federal court level in order to obtain leave to extend the period. That will cost $250. I have had experience of this with respect

to the Immigration Appeal Board, and I say it is a damnable shame to fix the time in such a way.
Let us consider what happens if there is an Air Canada strike. I should like to see the employees of Air Canada who were responsible for a damn fool strike pick up the tab for two people who are faced with a deportation order. They had to apply for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. They had to obtain the transcript of the hearing before the Immigration Appeal Board and a copy of the order. All these materials had to be shipped by pony express, so called, across Canada. May I say that that cost over $300 extra for these poor chaps, simply because the Immigration Appeal Board Act says that the period for appeal shall be ten days after the making of the order and the publishing of it in Ottawa.
We are now considering the same sort of thing. Why on earth do we always see this sort of capital city syndrome with regard to certain statutes. Why cannot administrative people be more accommodating and get up off their sterns, to put it frankly, and accommodate the citizen who is being affected, so that no matter whether a citizen lives in Lillooet, British Columbia, or Come-by-Chance, Newfoundland, he shall have ten days' notice, just as the person living in Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton or Ottawa does. I think it is downright unjust to draft statutes this way. To those who say to members representing districts some distance from Ottawa, "Oh, but you people always scream; you are cry babies," I say, if you go to the court for relief the individual concerned must pay the additional cost. I do not see why that should happen. I should like to hear the parliamentary secretary tell me what justification there is for continuing this unjustice that requires the period of the notice to run from the date of the mailing of the notice. The date of receipt is ignored.

Mr. Chairman, I waited for a moment to see if the parliamentary secretary would come forward with an amendment. I am prepared to move one if he is not so prepared. My amendment would be similar to one that was accepted previously. In that case, the requirement for ten days notice was altered to 30 days' notice. In this case, we are considering a serious penalty involving the right to seize personal chattels ten days after notice has been mailed by registered mail. For the reasons that my colleague has enumerated, I think it would be sensible to increase the period involved to 30 days, so that the person concerned can go to the bank and get the money for paying up his arrears, if that is what he wants to do. Surely, the ten day provision in this section is not less unfair than the ten day provision was in the previous section that was amended. In that case, a person had to launch an appeal within ten days of the mailing of the notice in Ottawa. In both cases, I submit, the ten day period would be unreasonable, and in one case an amendment was accepted.
If the government agrees with me, I will sit down. If not, I am prepared to move an amendment to alter the period in section 225 to 30 days. The parliamentary secretary indicates that I should proceed with my amendment. I will do so, Mr. Chairman.
I move:
That section 225 of clause 1 be amended at page 532 by striking out the figure 10 in line 22 and by substituting the figure 30.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have no objection at all to this amendment. I feel that measuring time from the date of mailing is the only practical solution; otherwise, we shall be involved in all manner of disputes as to when a particular letter is delivered, when it gets into the hands of the person concerned, if it ever gets there, and that sort of thing, or whether somebody else signed for the registered letter, and so on and so forth. That sort of problem is constantly encountered in the service of documents by mail.
However, the 30-day period should give ample protection to people in all parts of the country; taxpayers will be able to receive their notices in time and react to them, if they choose to do so. I think the hon. member's amendment is quite reasonable. I would not, however, agree with the hon. member for Edmonton West that it would be practical, however desirable it might be in theory, to depart from the time of mailing as the time from which we shall measure the beginning of the period in question.

Mr. Chairman, I think this amendment will go a long way towards meeting the objections that I have. However, the parliamentary secretary's practice of law must not involve much litigation. After all, most of the service of documents of the courts in his city is done by double registered mail. Certainly on matters of much greater import than this, such as a foreclosure, the documentation is always served by double registered mail. That is the only way. It never causes any particular inconvenience.
I have always found it very difficult to understand the so-called administrative difficulties in the Department of Justice. The provincial authorities have had a reasonably happy experience with double registered mail. This must mean that the people in the federal Department of Justice do not have any faith in the Post Office and that is why they turn down the idea of double registered mail. I know some of them will privately agree that they do not have any faith in it, but publicly they have to put on a much better face than that. By making the period 30-days, there is sufficient latitude and I am quite satisfied there is. I thank the parliamentary secretary for accepting this proposal, albeit I think it an imperfect solution.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had been about to make some comments on this when I heard my hon. friend's amendment. I am inclined to go along with it. The parliamentary secretary need not worry about there being any division. The parliamentary secretary said this is what the department deems it to be. I have no doubt that this is their intention. Are there judicial decisions which have been given? The parliamentary secretary is now being briefed on this, so I will not repeat what I said.

speechtext: On the specific point, Mr. Chairman, I am instructed that the Interpretation Act provides for this matter and the date of mailing is not included in the time period. The day immediately following the day of mailing is day one.

speechtext:
That is right.
Amendment (Mr. Aiken) agreed to.
Clause 1, section 225, as amended, agreed to.

In section 225(2) we have a further 10-day period for the keeping of goods after seizure. I wonder what the experience has been there. I am looking to the departmental officials to tell us whether they have encountered difficulties or criticisms in the courts from the rather short period because, if memory serves me correctly, I believe that under provincial statute seizures must be retained for longer than 10 days. The charges for storage and so on are the debtor's or the taxpayer's expense. Dealing with the outer reaches, is 10 days frankly adequate from the taxpayers' point of view?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the 10-day period here is the period during which the property is kept at the cost or expense of the taxpayer. At the end of that period, of course, the Crown is at liberty to proceed to the public auction. However, any costs or expenses incurred in retaining the seized chattel beyond the 10-day period is at the expense of the taxpayer. The length of time does not seem to be inappropriate. At this particular point, the taxpayer is very well aware of what is happening and has certainly had every opportunity to avail himself of whatever legal recourse he chooses. The limitation of 10 days is basically to assure that the taxpayers costs are not run up, as well as to give a decent period of time for him to take whatever action he needs to take, if he wants to redeem the goods.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The question asked by the hon. member for Edmonton West did not re-open the discussion on section 225 which was adopted as amended. We will now go to section 231.
On clause 1-section 231: Investigations.
Just a minute, Mr. Chairman. You are going a little fast.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Edmonton West said the Chair goes too fast. The Chair is trying to follow the directions of the committee which flow from the agreement accepted earlier.

Mr. Chairman, I am just rising to hold the fort for the hon. member for Edmonton West. Section 231 is one of the sections the hon. member asked to have stood at the last hearing. I believe he referred particularly to subsections (2) and (15), and perhaps other subsections.
I have some comments on these two subsections. The first comment relates to subsection (2) which requires the minister, within 120 days from the date of seizure of documents, records and papers, to return them to the person from whom they were seized. This is a long period of time to hold documents when copies can be made in a few minutes of any documents which may be relevant to a
Income Tax Act
prosecution. This provision could result in a tremendous loss to a person who had documents seized, particularly if he were trying to carry on a business and the documents seized were essential to his business. It comes to a halt. Not only can he not defend himself on the charges that may be brought against him because his documents have all been seized, but in the meantime he may go out of business. It seems that 120 days is an unreasonable length of time to hold these documents.
At this time I should like also to refer to subsection (15) of section 231 which reads:
Any person whose affairs are investigated in the course of an inquiry authorized under subsection (7) is entitled to be present and to be represented by counsel throughout the inquiry unless the hearing officer appointed under subsection (8) in relation to the inquiry, on application by the minister or a person giving evidence, orders otherwise in relation to the whole or any part of the inquiry on the ground that the presence of the person and his counsel, or either of them, would be prejudicial to the effective conduct of the inquiry.
I do not see how one could consider the presence of a person who is being investigated as prejudicial to the inquiry. I think it should be a basic right which should not be taken away by the person holding the inquiry. I can see no reason why a person so charged should not be present. If the department believes there are such circumstances, I would be pleased to hear an explanation. But the exception might then become the rule. Whoever is appointed to hold the board of inquiry might feel that the person whose affairs are being investigated would become a nuisance if he were allowed to be present. He might ask too many questions, raise too many points of order, and so on. As I say, I can see no justification on grounds of fairness for excluding from the hearing the person whose affairs are under investigation, or his counsel.

Mr. Chairman, I raised one or two questions on Tuesday last with regard to section 231 and the parliamentary secretary who was conducting the bill suggested we should stand the section.
I have been looking at the record. I think I did refer to section 231. We are again on 231(3). Notice is given or a demand is made by registered letter, and no specified period is set out, I want to know what is the period that is related to registered letters in matters of this kind. We were just looking at notice by way of registered letter and the period there was ten days. We are again getting a demand by way of registered letter and what is the time that is allowed by practice because there is no stated time under 231(3). If a registered letter is satisfactory to establish that a demand has been made in this particular case, why was a registered letter not administratively possible to use as I had suggested under section 225? It seems to me that in one case this is all right, but in the other case administratively it would be difficult. Frankly, I think before the courts one is faced with the same problem, proof of notice. If merely the mailing of a registered letter is sufficient to establish notice, I find that very difficult to understand.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
If there is a customary or common period, I will find out and let the hon. member know in a few moments.
With regard to the question raised by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka, there is no doubt that to have

December 6, 1971
Income Tax Act
records tied up for 120 days can be a great inconvenience to a taxpayer. However, the taxpayer does have full right of inspection during the period. It is the practice to permit him to make copies and extracts. I believe the hon. member's recollection of the laws of evidence will confirm my statement that original documents are most desirable as evidence when they are available, and that copies would not be as satisfactory in the case of the department deciding to proceed. From a practical point of view of any taxpayer going out of business as a result of this procedure, if the hon. member has any example of a taxpayer going out of business as a result of this procedure to cite in support of his speculation we should like to hear about it.
With regard to his statement that he cannot imagine circumstances in which a person should be excluded from a hearing under section 231(15) I would point out that this refers to inquiries authorized under subsection (7) for any purpose related to the administration or enforcement of the act. These are not simply inquiries into a taxpayers' affairs with a view to determining possible tax evasion or tax due on unreported revenue. This could involve situations where officials of the department have been bribed, or offered bribes. It could involve many aspects of the administration or maladministration of the act and, in circumstances of that sort, it might very well be necessary to undertake a closed inquiry. The hon. member will appreciate that any prosecutions would proceed in court after the result of the inquiry had been made known. In other circumstances, the taxpayer involved might be an employer. Evidence might be needed from his employees and there might be a possibility of intimidation. In the circumstances, the inquiry officer might decide that the taxpayer being investigated should not be present in order that the interests of justice might best be served.
What we are considering here is a new subsection. Previously, these investigations were all held without the person being investigated having the right to attend the inquiry. There are many situations involving the administration of the act in which an inquiry might be necessary, and at which the person being investigated ought not to be present.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the parliamentary secretary has taken a very interesting position. I can understand that there is a distinction to be made between a departmental investigation involving, possibly, issues such as bribery, intimidation and so on and other cases involving taxpayers directly, but I would have thought such cases could have been brought outside the scope of

subsection (7). The subsection is a new one, as is subsection (8) and subsection (15). This involves the consideration of who will be the hearing officers. Will they be from the public service? Will they be departmental people? If so, I agree thoroughly with my hon. friend from Parry Sound-Muskoka. I think it is altogether improper and unethical to give a judicial function to a government employee. Then, within the judicial capacity given by this section, the government official who is the hearing officer could, completely within his own discretion, refuse to allow the person whose affairs are being investigated in the course of an inquiry to be present and represented by counsel.
Now, quite obviously if the people whose conduct is being investigated, that may be allright. However, I believe there should be some distinction made here between people in that category and taxpayers. I think it should be quite plain there is no intention by this subsection to say to taxpayers that they cannot be present and cannot be represented by counsel because the hearing officer so decides. The parliamentary secretary has said that the intent is to make this distinction, and I gather from him that he feels there will not be a situation where a taxpayer in respect of whom an investigation is being conducted by a hearing officer will, in fact, be excluded or in fact not be allowed to be represented by counsel.
I think it is a matter of wording this so the plain distinction is drawn between two types of persons whose affairs are being investigated. It should be made absolutely plain in so far as taxpayers are concerned that when their affairs are being investigated that there is the right of appearance by counsel or personal appearance. I think possibly the parliamentary secretary might consider it in that light.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should point out that under subsection 8 the hearing officer is appointed by the tax review board on application by the minister. It would be contemplated that, in the ordinary course of events in the investigation of a taxpayer's affairs, this would be an independent person and not an officer of the department. I find it difficult to imagine the circumstances under which the tax review board would agree that that type of investigation could be appropriately carried out by an officer of the Department of National Revenue who in essence is one of the parties to the dispute. I think we can and should rely on the tax review board to see that it appoints appropriate people as these inquiry officers.

Mr. Chairman, in view of what the parliamentary secretary has said, and in view of the other arguments presented, I would make a suggestion to see how the government would react to it. I believe it would meet both points which have been raised. The parliamentary secretary has said there may be parts of an inquiry which do not relate directly to an individual or a certain person and it might be felt that he should not be present. However, if a person is to be excluded from such a hearing, I believe the grounds should be clear and that the onus should be on the hearing officer to establish that nothing will proceed in the absence of that person which affects him. I am wondering if it would be acceptable if all
December 6, 1971

the words after the word "inquiry" in line five were deleted and the words "so far as it relates to such person" substituted. In that case a hearing officer would have to determine whether or not the proceedings or the portion of the proceedings then going forward related to such a person, and the onus would be on the hearing officer- and also to guide himself during the absence of such person-not to deal with the rights of such a person under inquiry in his absence. I think such an amendment would alleviate the possibility which concerns us at the moment. I am throwing out this suggestion.
I repeat that everything after the word "inquiry" in line five should be deleted and that the words "so far as it relates to such person" be substituted. I should like to hear the reaction of the government on that proposal, because I think it would meet the problem which has been posed in respect of parts of an inquiry which do not relate to the person concerned but which relate to some departmental practice or procedure.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is quite true, Mr. Chairman, but the hon. member's amendment would nullify the whole section because at the point at which it involves the departmental practice or procedure, presumably the person being investigated is the departmental officer who is alleged to have been corrupt or corrupted. I think that the hon. member should realize that unless the inquiry were to take account of irrelevant or extraneous matters, the person investigated would inevitably be affected.

Then you have destroyed your whole argument that there is any point at which the evidence would be irrelevant. If as the parliamentary secretary says every part of the inquiry would relate to such a person, then why should he be excluded? I thought his argument was the other way around.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman. I think Judge Hoffman could outline situations for the hon. member where it would be essential that the party be excluded for good reason in order to effectively carry out the hearings. These things do happen. They have happened in our own country in cases some of which are still sub judice and which we cannot discuss. However, there are special circumstances in which it might be advisable, in the interest of justice, that the person be present or be represented by counsel. I have outlined some of these before. I have to go back to the fact that this is an inquiry officer appointed by the Tax Review Board and not an officer from the Department of National Revenue who is making this decision. The decision can be made only on application either by the minister or by some witness who is appearing before the inquiry. It is not one that the inquiry officer can institute. So I believe there are built-in checks. I believe we have indicated the policy desired that these people be present or represented wherever possible. I have also pointed out that these are administrative proceedings. This is an inquiry.
What happens in the judicial sense will depend on the resolution of that inquiry and will be disposed of in the ordinary courts of the land, in the Tax Review Board and so on. Frankly, my sense of justice is not offended by this provision. I think it is a very positive and new provision in the bill which will give rights which heretofore have not
Income Tax Act
been enjoyed by taxpayers. I think perhaps it is overdue, but I do not believe this particular subsection offends any basic principle of justice.

Mr. Chairman, I find it rather difficult to follow the parliamentary secretary at this point. As he said this is a new section. I cannot say that I am satisfied that the administrative practices under this section have been good because there have been no administrative practices under this particular section. On the other hand, I must say that I complimented the President of the Treasury Board the other day, and through him the government, for introducing the concept that the person involved could either be present or be represented by counsel when his affairs are being examined. Naturally, I did not say anything about the proviso. After all, the right that is being recognized is new. Then, there is the proviso according to which, the parliamentary secretary tells us, the minister must apply. But to whom must he apply in order to exclude the taxpayer and or his counsel? The hearing officer is appointed by the minister himself.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: By the Tax Review Board.

If the parliamentary secretary will look at subsections (7) and (8) he will see that the person who may be appointed a hearing officer may or may not be an employee of the Department of National Revenue. The person appointed is subject to confirmation by an order of the Tax Review Board.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: May I clarify this? Under subsection (7), the person appointed to conduct an inquiry may or may not be an officer of the department. He is analogous to the prosecuting attorney, if you like. Then, the hearing officer before whom the inquiry is conducted is appointed under subsection (8), and he is analagous to the judge, if I may make that analogy. He is the one who is appointed by the Tax Review Board. So, there are two different people.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Does the parliamentary secretary not contemplate that on the application to the Tax Review Board the minister will nominate a person and that when he applies, by means of whatever procedure would be adopted, he would say to the Tax Review Board "I am requesting the appointment of a hearing officer and I suggest such-and-such a person." I am not suggesting that this will be the course pursued, but I would like the parliamentary secretary to say that there is no intent on the part of the department for the minister to nominate the hearing officer.
Secondly, while the parliamentary secretary is considering that, let me refer to the point raised by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka. While I realize that any commitments or statements made in this House are not binding in a court of law, nevertheless perhaps the parliamentary secretary might indicate that it is the intent of the government, in dealing with subsection (15) and its implementation, not to deprive a taxpayer whose affairs are being investigated of the right to be present and represented by counsel. Is he able to give that reassurance that that is the intent and the practice which will be observed so far as the department is concerned.

December 6, 1971
Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
May I say on the first point that I think the Tax Review Board would be most reluctant to appoint an officer of the Department of National Revenue as the hearing officer in an investigation involving a dispute between a taxpayer and the department. I can visualize circumstances where the subject matter of the inquiry is departmental administration rather than a dispute between a taxpayer and the department where it might be appropriate, although I think that a competent, independent person would be more appropriate in almost any case.
On the second point, I cannot give the assurance for the simple reason that the inquiry officer will have to decide under subsection (15) that:
-the presence of the person and his counsel, or either of them, would be prejudicial to the effective conduct of the inquiry.
I do not have the imagination to be able to say that that would not occur in the case of an inquiry into the affairs of a taxpayer. I hope it would not occur often. The intent is that the person be allowed to be present or to be represented by counsel in all cases, and only when it is prejudicial to the inquiry does the presiding officer who is appointed by the Tax Review Board come to be called upon to make the decision to exclude the person. But circumstances might very well dictate to him that the ends of justice and the purpose of the inquiry would be best served by excluding him. That is why the option is there for the officer to make that ruling.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: To sum it up then, there are no guidelines. The hearing officer has the power, without any direction from the statute, to exclude on his own discretion a taxpayer and or his counsel from an inquiry.

It was very interesting to hear the observations of the parliamentary secretary and to hear him say that he did not think the special hearing officer would be an employee of the Department of National Revenue. It should not be too strange if the practice were adopted, because under the Immigration Act when a prospective immigrant to this country who wishes to be landed is examined by an immigration officer as to his qualifications for being landed and is then turned down, the appeal is by way of a special inquiry under a special inquiry officer who may be a fellow employee of the Department of Manpower and Immigration, in the same blessed branch, and who is asked to rule upon a prior decision of his colleague. That is why there are 7,500 cases before the Immigration Appeal Board now. I hope that at the appropriate time the appropriate minister may make the necessary changes in this respect. This is why there is this built-in abuse where one man is asked to rule on a prior decision of his colleague. This is what we find when we read the transcripts. I am not discussing the Immigration Act and the practices thereunder, but what I am saying is that this can happen within the realm of government administration and it is conceivable that certain officers of the Department of National Revenue could be recommended as special hearing officers. There is nothing to prevent this.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I admire the confidence of the parliamentary secretary. Let me say that many things are done in this House which have a different impact outside the House than was contemplated. I can recall the early days

of my practice of law in Peace River. At that time under the Fisheries Act-it may still be there for all I know and I am sorry the Minister of Fisheries has left the House-an enforcement officer of the Department of Fisheries could investigate alleged infractions against the Fisheries Act, lay a charge, appear as the justice of the peace, and try the case. The parliamentary secretary smiles.
I remember raising this point during the course of a dispute before the officer of the Fisheries Department who thought he had every right to do this. He was indignant that I would suggest it was not the thing to do, and finally I had to proceed by way of certiorari and have the conviction quashed. But I am quite convinced that when the House of Commons was discussing this particular clause some minister attempted to sooth the doubts and anxieties of members of the opposition by saying, "This does not mean anything. No one would operate in this way under it." But the facts of life are that when these powers are given, officials act under them and injustices do occur.
I am not going to say any more. I did contemplate moving an amendment. The government seems to be in a very flexible position today regarding amendments but I will not try my luck. When one considers the extent to which these provisions will be reflected in actual practice, one can see there is ample scope for grave injustices. I repeat that injustices will occur, and before too long a period has elapsed these sections will have to be amended along the lines that we have suggested. Certainly after the next election, when we form the government, we will do it if it has not been done before then.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I certainly do not want to filibuster this worthy section, but I would not wish to see the debate on this particular point terminate with any aspersions directed towards the Tax Review Board, which is a judicial body, and which is the body charged with appointing this person who conducts the inquiry, the hearing officer. I am confident that this board can be expected to exercise its powers of appointment as well as its powers in other respects in a judicial fashion. I have every confidence that this is a very progressive step and will not be abused.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
So far as I can see this step is far more conservative than progressive. No one is casting aspersions on the Tax Review Board, but it is my experience through long professional life of having to combat people engaged in the administration of government that, for what they deem to be good and sufficient purposes and reasons, they have no objection to utilizing all the scope of ambiguously worded sections of this kind, which grant great powers, and that under those conditions injustices occur.
I will leave it at that, Mr. Chairman. I think the parliamentary secretary is wrong. I think the situation is much different from what he contemplates, and I prophesy that these powers will be abused. We have done our job as a responsible opposition. We have directed the attention of the committee to the dangers which exist. Having done that, and having filed our caveat, if the government insists
December 6, 1971

on passage of these provisions without any amendment then the responsibility rests on it.

Mr. Chairman, I think there is a very important principle involved here. That is why I wish to support the position taken by the hon. member for Edmonton West and the hon. member for Peace River. All of us can recall that when Department of Veterans Affairs legislation was being debated here some months ago, one of the important principles then established was that of a separate and distinct appellate division. It was the feeling that if the person called upon to conduct a review was, in effect, the same person or administrative body that made the decision in the first place, then the kind of problem mentioned by the hon. member for Peace River had a greater chance to arise, and discrimination could occur.
On behalf of a number of my constituents I have made requests for review boards to various ministries, including National Health and Welfare, Manpower and Immigration, National Defence and others. In most cases I have found that an independent review takes place, but in others I had a strong suspicion that the review was conducted by the people, or friends of the people who made the decision in the first place, and that they were content to defend the original decision. The reason for the existence of any appellate court is to provide an open and fresh look at a particular problem. I think this is best achieved if the party first involved in the decision making is not connected with the review.

speechtext: Is the committee ready for the question?
Mr. Chairman, I do not know if the parliamentary secretary wishes to reply to the hon. member who has just spoken, but if not we could proceed with the voting.

speechtext:
