On clause 1-section 235: Penalty for failure to make returns.
Income Tax Act

Mr. Chairman, section 235 is tied in with section 239, and I want to hear the reply to my amendment to section 239. Actually 235 is the present counterpart to 239 (2), because 235 says it is an offence under the act to fail to file a return under certain subsections, and 235(2) sets out other circumstances under which a person who fails to act in accordance with regulations passed under authority of "paragraph 221" may be prosecuted.
First of all, what about the regulations? Are they ready? I see looks of surprise among some of the officials. If they had been present last week they would know whereof I speak, because at that time I questioned whether certain regulations were ready since they have just as much import with regard to the administration of the act as do the statutory provisions.
Section 235 is a classic example. It is conceivable that these are merely a carry forward of section 129(1)(2) of the present act and that there are regulations in existence with regard to them. As I have pointed out again and again, however, this is a new act. All is on the table, including the regulations. I want to know if it is proposed to make any new regulations, or are they to be the same as heretofore in regard to section 235?
I spoke about sections 235 and 239. Under section 235, for instance, it is an offence to fail to file a return, and it may be very important that returns are consistently not made following demands-as an open defiance of the act and perhaps a suppression of revenues-but the penalty provided is on summary conviction. Mr. Chairman, there is another provision which says that there can be another penalty. Section 239(1) lays out another type of penalty for non-compliance with the act. Subsection (2) says that anything that is in non-compliance of the act under subsection (1) may be the subject of an indictment. So an offence under section 235 could prove to be indictable.
I ask why the indictment procedure is upheld in some cases and not in others. As I said already in reference to section 239 (2), it is completely contrary to any sense of justice for a minister or official to decide that a man shall go to jail. That is the effect of section 239 (2) which I shall argue in due course. I have made my preliminary argument with regard to section 235. I have some preliminary questions in that respect, but the real thrust of what I want to get at is section 239 (2).

Mr. Chairman, there is one thing that particularly bothers me about the combination of sections 221 (2), 235 and 239. Under section 221 (2), to which we raised objection but on which we were overruled, regulations under the act shall, if the regulation so provides, be effective with reference to a period before it was published. We already have that on the books; the section has been passed. It seems to me that it meant that if there is a prosecution under section 235, which we are now considering, for failing to make a return as and, when required by regulation-under section 221-a person can be charged with committing an offence which did not exist at the time he committed it. In other words, the regulation can be backdated: it could be published on September 30, effective the previous June 30.

December 6, 1971
Income Tax Act
What would happen to a person who on July 30 failed to comply with a regulation which was not then promulgated or published? Under the combination of these three clauses he could be found guilty under section 235 and sent to jail for two months under section 239 for failing to comply with a provision under section 221 which did not exist at the time he breached it. This seems to me the most ridiculous part of the Income Tax Act that we have before us.
It is all very well to say that the Department of National Revenue would never do such a thing. I do not suppose anybody would intentionally do it, but I think it behooves members of this House to make sure that such a situation cannot happen and that we are passing sensible laws. This is an example of the most senseless group of sections I have ever seen. Section 221 was not well drafted, in view of sections 235 and 239; but I am afraid we cannot go back to section 221 as it has been passed. We cannot go back to section 221 (2) and I suppose I should not be reflecting on the vote, and I am not, any more than to say that since it has been accepted it has left us in a ridiculous situation with regard to sections 235 and 239.
Section 239 gives the minister the right to proceed by way of indictment against a person for failing to file a return under section 235. He proceeds by way of indictment and the penalty is a minimum of two months in jail. Section 235 specifically mentions regulations under section 221 which can be promulgated and become effective before they are even published or made known to the public. Ignorance of the law is no excuse-but surely ignorance of a law which does not at that time exist, ignorance of a law which at that time is not known to the public, has not been promulgated and has not been published, should be a defence. Yet that is not the way in which this combination of sections has been drawn. From the beginning we objected to the absolute right of the minister to proceed by way of indictment under section 235 particularly, which can be nothing more than failure to file a return.
To carry the argument further, the offence could amount to nothing more than failure to file a return in the prescribed form. If the regulation is introduced on September 30, to be effective on July 30, there is no way that a person could comply with it. But he could be sent to jail for two months for non-compliance. If my reasoning is wrong, I should like to have it corrected.
I have looked at this matter in connection with sections 239 and 221. I do not see how the department can justify section 239(2) in concert with section 235-the section we are considering-unless 239 is amended in the manner proposed by the hon. member for Edmonton West. If accepted, the question of sentence would be left to the presiding judge, and the minister merely on his own authority would not be permitted to proceed by way of indictment. The judge would have to determine the circumstances of the case in sentencing. Frankly, I am not even prepared to go that far. There are some judges whom I would not trust, either. I will not name them, but I would not trust them any more than I would trust the government. I have appeared before them.

If the present provisions of the bill become law, judges will have no option but to convict. I can almost hear a judge saying to an accused, "I know that this is a ridiculous situation, but I am required by the law to convict you and send you to jail for two months for failing to file a return, which requirement did not exist at the time you were supposed to file the return." What can a judge do? He will have no option but to enforce a ridiculous provision in the law. I will say no more until the parliamentary secretary tells me that there is something wrong with my argument and that what I have suggested cannot take place.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I do not believe, Mr. Chairman, that it is within the power of the Governor in Council by regulation to create retroactive criminal consequences. I think the hon. member contemplates that this might happen. I am advised that that is beyond the power of the Governor in Council and that the courts would not uphold such regulations.

Then why did we pass section 221(2) which provides:
No regulation made under this act has effect until it has been published in the Canada Gazette but, when so published, a regulation shall, if it so provides, be effective with reference to a period before it was published.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is contemplated that there will be necessity for numerous regulations to have retroactive effect after this act has been implemented, in order to make sure that there is no punitive impact on taxpayers as a result of the transitional period. It is anticipated that these retroactive regulations will be relieving in nature. It is certainly not contemplated that punitive regulations will be passed. Indeed, as I indicated earlier, such punitive regulations would not be legal if they were passed.
We recognize the necessity for relieving regulations. For example, let us consider the instance, raised earlier and debated at some length, involving the B.C. teachers and the credit union-a matter in which the hon. member for Edmonton West took great interest. In that case it would be necessary to pass a regulation that would be retroactive to budget day so that the type of investment these people have been making will be a qualified investment for the purposes of their pension plan. That is the sort of thing that is contemplated.

I appreciate what the intention may be, but regardless of all these fine intentions the act specifies that regulations can be published and be effective prior to the publication date. The situation I alluded to could arise. What I am trying to do is to include a provision, either under section 235 which we are now considering, or section 239 which will prevent the suggested situation from arising and which the parliamentary secretary says is not likely to happen. If in the future section 221 is deemed to be illegal, or if regulations passed under that section are found to be illegal, why should we pass such regulations now? Why should we not include in the bill a saving provision?
The parliamentary secretary has suggested that we must pass retroactive regulations now because they will all be retroactive to the date on which the bill will become
December 6, 1971

effective. I am objecting to passing regulations which will not be in existence at the time of a prosecution. I think we should make sure, either by amendment to section 235 or to section 239, that such situation cannot arise. The parliamentary secretary has suggested that you cannot legally pass retroactive criminal legislation. I do not agree with him. Talking off the top of my head, I suggest that we often pass criminal retroactive legislation.
That is how the public order bill worked.

Yes. When we passed the Public Order (Temporary Measures) Act it was to be effective on a date prior to its implementation. I also cite the War Measures Act. That act was invoked by order in council and Parliament approved it some days later. It could not have been approved in a form different from that in which it was proposed.
I have given two examples but I can think of many others to show that we have passed criminal legislation and dated it back, so to speak. That is why section 239(2) is so dangerous. It gives the minister the right to proceed by way of indictment in the sort of situation to which I have alluded. I cannot understand why that should be done. We have not yet dealt with section 239, but since we are dealing with these matters perhaps the parliamentary secretary would reassure us concerning the amendment to section 239 which the hon. member for Edmonton West has moved. Is he prepared to accept this or a simiar amendment? If he is, some of the dangers I have outlined may be eliminated.

Mr. Chairman, notwithstanding all the pious hopes of the parliamentary secretary and protestations regarding the good behaviour in future of the administrative people, I think that what the parliamentary secretary said is, frankly, fatuous. The parliamentary secretary said that no government or administration would make retroactive legislation that has a penal effect. Then what in the blazes is he talking about in section 235? Section 235 provides:
Every person who has failed to make a return as and when required by regulation under subsection 215(4), by regulation under section 221-
It does not say section 221(1) or 221(2); it says section 221. That means all the section.
-or by subsection 227(2) is liable to a penalty of $10 a day for each day of default but not exceeding in all $2,500.
In other words, the regulations under section 221 can, and specifically do, create an offence under the act. Section 235(2) provides:
Every person who fails to comply with a regulation made under paragraph 221 (l)(e)-
Section 221(l)(e) provides:
-required to make an information return to supply a copy of the information return or of a prescribed portion thereof to the person or persons in respect of whose income the information return or portion thereof relates.
In other words, it is with regard to his employees. If he fails to do that, he can be fined $10 a day up to a maximum of $2,500. That is non-compliance with the act. As I
Income Tax Act
have said, anything which is made an offence under section 235 is ipso facto an offence under section 239(1). Under section 239(1) there is full authority to proceed against the individual by way of indictment. As the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka said, the net result is a regulation and it is spelled out in section 235. Any kind of regulation can be made with a retroactive effect requiring compliance. Within the neutral period there could be noncompliance. This then becomes an offence under the law, with the consequences I have pointed out.
Let no one say we are stretching things. If there is not to be any offence created, and if it is not the intention to use the section for that purpose, it is not required within the law. That is simple. Therefore, why this confusion? I want the parliamentary secretary to tell us that what we are suggesting cannot in fact happen. He can say that he does not think it will happen. But it is very possible it can. The language is clear. It is absolutely possible for it to happen. Therefore, it should not be in the act.

Mr. Chairman, I wish we could get some assurance on this section before we pass it. I am not ready to let section 235 pass until we know where we are going on section 239. We have not yet had an answer. It is almost six o'clock. Perhaps the parliamentary secretary would like to consider the position over the dinner hour. This is a serious point. It is the basis of the whole administration and enforcement section of the Income Tax Act.
All the other things are there, the whole 700 pages, but the administration and enforcement of it are contained within the three sections we are now considering. We would be irresponsible if we permitted this section to be passed into law without a good deal more assurance than we now have. Either section 235 or section 239(2) requires amendment. If the government clearly states it does not intend that any prosecution shall proceed under a regulation which is promulgated subsequent to an alleged offence having been committed, all they have to do is write it into the income tax bill and we will be happy.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. It being six o'clock, I do now leave the chair.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: When the committee rose at six o'clock we were discussing section 235.

I rise merely to ask the parliamentary secretary whether the government has anything to offer the committee with regard to the problems we raised this afternoon in connection with sections 235, 221 and 239(2).

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I wish I could satisfy the hon. member better than I am sure I shall be able to do. First, I must take some exception to the suggestion he made before dinner that I had not responded to his questions earlier. I believe I did respond, though I can understand that he

December 6, 1971
Income Tax Act
might not be satisfied with the answers I gave. But that is another question. We are dealing here with an area of the bill which, frankly, does not lend itself to the provision of the happy answers I might otherwise be able to supply. Experience of enforcement indicates that we require these sections very much unchanged.
We have no amendments to put forward, neither have any amendments been forthcoming from elsewhere that we are prepared to accept. This is the sort of thing the hon. member for Edmonton West, in his previous position of parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Revenue, no doubt had to live with. I am sure at that time he presented to his minister many suggestions as to how the sections might be improved. The fact is that the sections before us are a carryover from the existing act. We feel that in the practical sense, in their practical application, there is little room for inequity. If there is, we shall be prepared to move and act accordingly.
Section 221 is not a new section and it is not a punitive section; it is one which is referred to in section 235. A number of the provisions in that section are new. They have been made in anticipation that regulations will be required to relieve taxpayers of unfair burdens during the transitional period. It is for this reason that we anticipate that regulations will be passed having a retroactive effect.
I realize that hon. members opposite can argue that regulations might be passed which would impose a burden of some description upon taxpayers on a retroactive basis. They can argue this in theory but in practice I do not think the courts would uphold any regulation which imposed a burden on taxpayers retroactively because, essentially, that would be the imposition of a tax, which is the prerogative of Parliament, and not of the Governor in Council. Again, I regret that my response is not likely to satisfy the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka or the hon. member for Edmonton West.

In that case, I suggest to the hon. gentleman that he look at the implications. He may say these are carryovers and have never given rise to any problems. But it is only in the past session that the House approved the Statutory Instruments Act. It would be an extremely interesting situation if the committee which will be set up at some time to review statutory instruments were to find that the effect of a regulation was totally unfair, though the minister might have been relying on the authority given him by the House to impose such a regulation.
This is the difficulty. Allowance has been made in section 221(2) for retroactive regulations. During the currency of the existing act there has been no such thing as the Statutory Instruments Act. The parliamentary secretary should remember what the Minister of Justice said when that act was passed-that orders in council or regulations would be subject to screening by the committee, and to adverse recommendations, if they applied with retroactive effect.
How does Parliament square-up a recommendation from a committee of the House which says that this regulation is bad in so far as it is retroactive. Yet the House has authorized retroactive regulations in this legislation. I
cannot square this up at all. I know the House has given approval to section 221(2), but the effect comes home in section 235 because that section speaks of section 221 and provides a penalty for an offence under any regulation passed pursuant to the whole of section 221.
I wonder whether the parliamentary secretary would be prepared to accept a proviso to section 235 in respect of section 221. As my colleague from Parry Sound-Muskoka indicated, there is good reason for section 221(2) in order to give effect to the provision that no regulation shall be effective until it has been published in the Canada Gazette, and to that part we say "Amen." We agree with that, but we do not agree that under section 235 there can be a penalty imposed on a taxpayer under the retroactive effect of section 221(2).
I am wondering whether we might insert a proviso within section 235 which would clearly eliminate any question of penalty. I admit the regulation would have to be effective, but there should be no penalty for an offence committed under a regulation before its publication, regardless of the effective date of the regulation. This is the point which bothers us in respect of this section. Is the parliamentary secretary prepared to accept an amendment? We would have to sit down and arrive at some careful wording here. However, that is the idea we want to get across. We want to eliminate any question of a penalty under the retroactive portion of the regulation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, while the parliamentary secretary is considering these weighty words I wish to reinforce what my hon. friend from Edmonton West has said. I sat on the statutory instruments committee. Before the bill came into the House a lengthy report was tabled by the committee and accepted. Everyone spoke glowing words about it and said what a wonderful report it was. It was unanimous. There was complete agreement on all sides of the House.
I suggest one of the essentials upon which the committee founded its report was that regulations should not have a retroactive effect. I was not in the House when section 221(2) was passed. My friends were here and of course made their comments about it. I am sure had I been here I would have spoken very strongly indeed, because here we have a report from the committee on statutory instruments, which sat for some time, received a lot of guidance had the benefit of the experience of the United Kingdom and Australia and finally brought in a report saying unanimously that regulations must not be retroactive in effect.
Here we have the case of Parliament going one way in respect of a report of the committee of the House, and the government going in the opposite direction by ignoring it and trying to pass two trains on one track. This section has been passed and nothing can be done about it. However, there will be an opportunity for the scrutiny committee to do something. Perhaps the parliamentary secretary would try to light a little fire under the appropriate part of the anatomy of his respective ministers in order to get the committee set up.
I would feel a little safer and worry less about the taxpayers of this country if there were in effect today a parliamentary scrutiny committee charged with examining regulations passed and which, under the terms of the

December 6, 1971

Statutory Instruments Act and pursuant to the very definite mandate given by the committee to this House, would look at a number of things including whether or not regulations passed should have a retroactive effect. I know there are ministers in the cabinet, some members on the government side-I except a lot of people here, but not all of them-and people in the administrative services who are very anxious about what will happen when this committee is created, in respect of the sins of omission and commission which have been discreetly covered over but are contained in regulations, amendments to regulations, orders in council and amendments to orders in council which rarely, if ever, see the light of day. A lot of people are concerned whether a committee will ever be established under the Statutory Instruments Act to look into this matter about which my hon. friend from Edmonton West has spoken.
I see the Acting Prime Minister sitting over there. I do not wish to provoke him into debate. He has been very patient in listening to me and my hon. friends, and I hope he is learning something. But I should like him to stand up and say that before this session ends the government will establish a joint committee under the Statutory Instruments Act so that when we come to situations where regulations are passed pursuant to Bill C-259 which have a retroactive effect and under which retroactively people can be punished, fined or sent to jail, there will be a scrutiny committee to pay attention to governmental misdemeanours and, I hope, challenge the government and bring the matter back to Parliament for debate and reconsideration. That is the purpose of such a committee.
For months I have been attempting to get this committee established. We are prepared to deliver our list of nominees to this committee. An additional reason now is the bill before the House and the regulations which permit the government to do these things. These things might be done for the very best of reasons, but it is iniquitous, wrong and vicious to have a situation where a government can by regulation put people in a position where they will be punished by fine and/or imprisonment for having committed an offence prior to the enactment of the regulation. For this reason, if the government is not prepared to change this provision and accept the reasoned and logical arguments of my friends, I hope they will recognize the problem and be prepared to expedite the establishment of the statutory instruments committee for the purpose of looking at the problems created by this section.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
First, I do understand that the Statutory Instruments Act has been proclaimed and will become operative on the first of next year. Therefore, any regulations that are likely to be passed under the act will be passed subsequent to the Statutory Instruments Act coming into force, and there is no reason of which I am aware to think that the regulations passed under this act will not be subject to the scrutiny that the hon. member for Peace River has indicated.
Second, we are most reluctant to concede that there is an opportunity under this bill to pass punitive regulations with retroactive effect, and for that reason we have no amendment to propose, However, I say very sincerely to the hon. member for Edmonton West and the hon.
Income Tax Act
member for Parry Sound-Muskoka that if they have an amendment to propose to this section which would improve the position from their point of view and solve the problem as they see it, we will certainly look at it very seriously.
However, it is our position that any regulations passed under this legislation that would have a punitive effect on any taxpayer retroactively would be ultra vires of the delegated authority given under this bill. I want to make that very clear. That is the reason we do not want, by any amendment that we might offer, to imply that such regulations could indeed have any force and effect. However, I will await with interest any amendment proposed by hon. members and we will certainly consider it seriously. I think hon. members have acknowledged in their general comments that this is a complex problem. I would not be prepared to see their amendment voted on immediately it is proposed, but we will certainly look at it seriously and if it is not acceptable to the government we will have a reasoned argument for rejecting it.

I accept that there can be a need for section 221 (2), but where I do not want it to have effect is in a punitive section such as section 235 which we are considering. Therefore, I suggest on reflection that notwithstanding the fact that the road to Hades is paved with good intentions-and I know these are all good intentions of the parliamentary secretary-the punitive feature in a regulation would not be ultra vires of the fact; it would not impose an additional tax but it could be justified on the basis of the existence of section 221 (2) which gives full power to pass a retroactive regulation- and Parliament has consciously made a decision on that matter. Therefore, with regard to section 235 I move:
That subsection 235 (1) at page 547 be amended by deleting in line 22 the figures 221 and substituting therefor 221 (1).
Under section 221 there is all the power and specification of the type of regulation that can be made. Under section 235 there would be no penalty or retroactive feature because 221 (2) gives retroactive effect to a regulation. I know this will require some study but I make this motion, if it is accepted by the Chair, for consideration by departmental officials at the appropriate time.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Hon. members have heard the motion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Certainly, we take no procedural objection to this amendment and unless there is further comment on the section we ask that it be stood overnight to permit the law officers to consider it and to give any legal advise that may be desirable.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is it agreed that section 235 and the amendment be stood at this time?

Agreed.
Clause 1, section 235, stood.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The committee will now proceed with section 239, on which there is an amendment by the hon. member for Edmonton West.
On clause 1-section 239: Offences.

December 6, 1971
Income Tax Act

I do not think I need add much more on this section because we argued it at great length the other night and we argued it at considerable length this afternoon. However, I wish to reiterate some points for the great number of hon. members who are in the committee tonight. We are appreciative of the fact that the lash seems to have been imposed with effect last Thursday, and that gracing the House tonight are more cabinet members than we had during the question period. They are gainfully employed this evening.
I do not think there is one hon. member across the way who would want to be in the position of the minister who has to decide whether a taxpayer shall go to jail. The Minister of Justice, as Attorney General for Canada, has the right to do that under section 239 (2) because non-compliance with the act within the terms of the section is a matter of fact. Wilfully refusing to file a return demands a great number of actions under section 239. These are matters of fact. There is no question that there may be other than a finding of guilty or a plea of guilty, yet by the minister proceeding through the indictment route there is a mandatory jail sentence.
I put this case to anybody who has had any connection with the Department of National Revenue or the Department of Justice. Some time ago I had three years' connection with one of those departments. At that time it was the Minister of National Revenue who decided these matters, not the Attorney General. As soon as it became apparent to a taxpayer that the government was likely to proceed by the indictment route, you could bet your bottom dollar that the next morning a friend of a friend of a friend of the taxpayer was on the telephone to the minister, putting the pressure on him not to go by the indictment route because the individual involved would have to go to jail. I defy any member opposite to say he wants to be put in the position of a minister who is under pressure to decide whether a particular non-compliance with the act must result in the defaulting taxpayer going to jail.
My amendment would provide for proceeding by way of summary conviction with the judge, usually a provincial judge in these cases, having the power to impose a sentence of up to five years imprisonment, which is what is provided in section 239 (2). Already under section 239(1) the judge has power to impose a fine or jail sentence, or both, but the limit is two years. Surely to goodness it is elementary justice that there is only one instrument to sentence a man to jail, and that is sentence after a court hearing, by a properly constituted judge from whom there is an appeal. Under the indictment procedure there is a mandatory jail sentence and there can be no appeal except as to the length of sentence.
Is the Income Tax Act to be that tough? In many respects it is tougher than the Criminal Code. Is that the kind of law we are asked to pass in this so-called enlightened day, when the Minister of Justice and his colleague the Solicitor General are talking about a more enlightened correctional policy and a more enlightened administration of justice? It is said that we in Canada are sending too many people to jail, yet in this instance we are being asked to provide a mandatory jail sentence for a taxpayer.
[The Deputy Chairman.]
The quantum of the fine must also be considered. Section 239(l)(f) provides for "a fine of not less than 25 per cent and not more than double the amount of the tax" involved, and there is also the possibility of a sentence of up to two years in jail. I provide in my amendment for an option of up to five years in jail, which is the penalty provided for in 239(2), where presumably in the past there was a special penalty reserved for the really bad boys. Why does the minister have to make the decision that a man shall go to jail? Why is it he or his officials who decide, by choosing the compulsory imprisonment route? I object to that.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if one stays around here a while he learns a lot of law, but I confess I have been finding the learning process in relation to this section a bit slow. I am not going to say anything to show my ignorance or to underline my difficulty, but I wish some of the lawyers in the House-and we have scads of them here tonight-would give a serious answer to the contention put forward by the hon. member for Edmonton West.
I confess that as I read the section it seems to me there still has to be a conviction by a court. In other words, it is the court that sends somebody to jail. Yet the hon. member for Edmonton West, who is a distinguished member of the Bar, has said a good many times that the way the act is set up it is the minister who decides that someone shall go to jail. If he is right, this is pretty bad. If he is not right, then I wish some of the distinguished members of the Bar on the other side would explain it. I am not trying to resolve the issue; I am just saying that as a neophyte in this area I would like to know what this argument is all about.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member for Edmonton West is both overdramatizing and oversim-plying the situation. It is not the Minister of Justice who decides whether someone will go to jail: that is a determination made by the courts.
What does happen is that the Minister of justice may determine in this particular case, as I understand he can in some others, that the matter is of such a serious nature that it should proceed by indictment rather than by summary conviction before a magistrate; in other words, that it must proceed by indictment to the Supreme Court. At that point the court must still decide, on the evidence presented to it, whether an offence has been committed and whether a conviction is warranted. Once the court decides that, then certainly this section does come into operation: it does provide a minimum penalty of two months' imprisonment. But it is not the Minister of Justice who determines whether a person is guilty or innocent, or what the penalty will be. That decision is the decision of the court.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in any criminal offence there are two elements. First, there is the question of guilt, and on it the minister can have no concern. That is for the court to determine. The second element in any criminal offence is that of punishment. In the kind of society in which we live, the question of punishment really becomes of equal importance-and sometimes even more important, particularly in tax laws-than the question of guilt.
December 6, 1971

Here we have a minister of the Crown making a judicial determination.
The minister of the Crown may say, "In my opinion and in my administrative capacity I have decided that the offence this person is to be charged with is so serious that it warrants a penalty of so many months or years in jail." That is a judicial determination. No minister and no administrative official should have that power. I agree that in evaluating whether the gravity of the offence and the surrounding circumstances warrant a man's going to jail is something that should be determined by a court. However, in this case the court has no alternative; the man must be sent to jail as a result of an administrative decision by the minister. I think that is a very simple point and I hope my friend from Winnipeg North Centre sees that distinction.
I saw that the hon. member for High Park, who is a lawyer of no mean distinction, was quite interested in this question and I would be glad to hear his opinion on it. I am sure he has the welfare of the ordinary person at heart and I think he will agree with me. I know that at one time he had some ideas about the right of a minister to make decisions of this kind. He might be willing to agree with me now or when a vote is called.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It is widespread practice under the Criminal Code, and it was at the time the hon. member's party formed the government, that you have this choice of proceeding by way of indictment or summary conviction. Is the hon. member suggesting that this choice ought to be taken out of the criminal statutes?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Each one to be considered on its merits. When this government brings before us the Criminal Code for general review, I think we will eliminate a lot of this problem.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: In all cases?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No, but in many cases. It should not be an administrative decision. If there were ever any ground for it, it certainly should not be a Liberal government that has to make the decision.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: What the hon. member is saying is that with regard to some offences under the Criminal Code he would leave the choice in there, but for middle-class crimes such as income tax the hon. gentleman does not want his friends to go to jail.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Does the hon. gentleman not recognize that with regard to punitive sections, so far as tax penalties go there is a difference. The rigid liquor control laws failed at one time in some parts of Canada for that very same reason-these alternatives were not given. We often find that when the state is involved and is worried about its revenues, it would much rather send a man to jail for
Income Tax Act
five years than impose a penalty more in line with that imposed for a similar criminal offence. This is a red herring, and the Minister of National Defence is a man of red herrings: he holds that distinction.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: This is a red herring, and it is a very ancient one because it smells mouldy.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, if it is a better question than the one asked by the Minister of National Defence.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is the hon. member for Hamil-ton-Wentworth rising on a point of order?
I wonder if my friend would permit a question.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I hope it is a better one than the last.

Without trying to score a debating point, and with respect, I wonder if my hon. friend is familiar with the decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal which recently decided an issue of this kind under the Bill of Rights. The discretion of the Crown was challenged because the Attorney General, through the Crown Attorney, was given the choice of proceeding by way of indictment or summary conviction in the case of Regina v. Smyth, who is now deceased. In that case the Court of Appeal came to the conclusion that despite the fact there was a more severe penalty by indictment than by summary conviction, the Crown had always had discretion to choose which form of prosecution it would use. I wonder if my friend is aware of that? If he had read that case he might have a different view.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
That was a judicial interpretation. The judges were saying what the law was, but I am saying what the law should be. I think it is time we got away from the position where we are putting rights of this kind in the hands of ministers of the Crown.
I go back to what my friend the Minister of National Defence said. There may be some circumstances under the Criminal Code where this discretion is necessary, but very few. I should like to see a complete review of the Criminal Code so that this improper discretion would be eliminated. This authority should not rest with administrative officials. If we have courts, if we have judges, if we have juries and give this right to them, we should not leave it in the hands of a minister. I would not want to see it in the hands of a minister who formed part of a Progressive Conservative government any more than I would want to see it in the hands of a minister who formed part of the Liberal government. I say nothing about my friends to the left because they will never form a government, so I do not need to worry about that.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Hon. members may laugh at this, but the time is coming when the people of this country will look askance at this kind of authority being given to a government to exercise its discretion. It is wrong and I think it is

Income Tax Act
time we stopped it. I am glad my hon. friend from Edmonton West raised this question and that we have a chance to make these points. I do not know whether we will have any amendments, but I suggest to my friends on the other side that they should look very seriously at this as a matter of principle as well as with respect to this particular issue.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Does the hon. member for High Park wish to ask a question?

Mr. Chairman, with all due respect to the hon. member for Peace River and the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth, I still ask, why does the Crown have the authority to choose which way we will proceed? It is wrong because that is imposing one law on one group of citizens and another law on another group. I agree with the hon. member for Peace River in this regard.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is the best argument I have heard today.

Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that we are getting into a philosophical question. I listened to some of the comments and would suggest that what we are doing in some instances is putting this income tax legislation above the Criminal Code. That is what troubles me. I wish to give only one example in this generally related group of sections. Section 243 says, "notwithstanding the Criminal Code or any other statute". It seems to me that this is a bad thing.
Another point along the same lines has been advanced from time to time by other hon. members, including the hon. member for High Park. I agree with his philosophy. In section 244 there is another example. Any criminal lawyer knows that there are certain defences open to an accused when an information is defective on its face. In this income tax legislation we see again that it does not make any difference how deficient, negligent or inappropriate an information may be, or how it is drawn-there is no way an accused can have the benefit of counsel pointing this out, under section 244.1 realize that we are talking about section 239 but it is all part of the same question.
It seems to me that we are getting into a situation where we are putting this proposed Income Tax Act above the Criminal Code. I think this is a fundamental matter and I do not think it is in the best interests of Canadians to have an act which is dictatorial and coercive to the extent this act appears to be, and above the Criminal Code.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I confess I am still thinking out loud and pursuing my study of the law. The remarks which have been made recently remind me that the criminal law of Canada is not, as I have been told a number of times, confined to the Criminal Code. As I understand it, a person stealing a loaf of bread or a few dollars is dealt with under the Criminal Code. It could be that here we may deal with people who defraud the country, that is the people of Canada and the treasury, of thousands of dollars because they make false entries, destroy records and do that kind of thing. Is not that kind of thing as much a crime as stealing a loaf of bread, stealing clothes from a store or stealing a few dollars?
We are with you, Stanley.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: We are presenting a united front.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Since the parliamentary secretary a moment ago, after the hon. member for High Park had spoken, said that was the best argument he had heard from the other side, I am beginning to wonder if I am on the wrong track.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: My friend from St. Boniface says I am on the right track, and that makes me wonder. Mind you, it is confusing seeing that phalanx of Liberals on the other side of the House. I think my friend from Edmonton West and others who have adopted his view raised something we should not overlook, the placing of dictatorial power in the hands of ministers. I do not know where my friends of the Conservative party were when we were complaining about the crackdown on some people who had broken the Unemployment Insurance Act. We felt that just as much effort should be made to make sure people get what they are entitled to as to catch people who commit an offence. Here we are dealing with very much wealthier people, with people who can save a great deal by defrauding the treasury.
In many instances they are small businessmen.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
The hon.
member says that in many instances they are small businessmen. Often, they are even smaller than that. From my reading of section 239, there is a long list of pretty serious crimes for which you could be penalized-crimes like false entries, deception, the burning and destroying of records and wilfully doing everything possible to avoid paying what is owing to the people of Canada.
And destroying ballots.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Destroying ballots? It is in Newfoundland where they destroy ballots. All these crimes I have enumerated are pretty serious crimes. There seems to be a choice as to penalties that will be imposed if this law is broken. If someone is convicted, he is liable, on summary conviction, to pay a fine of not less than 25 per cent and not more than 200 per cent of the tax that was sought to be evaded. If a little fellow is involved and the amount of tax is small, perhaps no great sum will be levied, even though he has committed a serious crime.
However, as I see it, in cases where there is a wholesale defrauding of the public treasury that runs to thousands or millions of dollars, it is proper for the law to say that in such cases action can be taken by way of indictment. I said when I began that I was trying to learn what this is all about. I have been listening to the hon. member for Edmonton West and those on the other side and I am glad that my questions have produced comments both ways. It seems to me that we must provide for penalties and for people to be taken to court for the crime of defrauding the treasury of Canada, in the same way as we have made provision for those who have stolen a few things from a store and I gather that that is what this section provides.

Mr. Chairman, it
appears that some hon. members have not read section 239(1). The Minister of National Defence has suggested that we are trying to protect the big fellow. I did not know he was interested in law of this kind since I understood he is more interested in international law, as he told a gathering of people the other day. I suggest to hon. members, and particularly to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for Winnipeg North who is sitting with him, that section 239(l)(a) deals with the little fellow who has been moonlighting and fails to disclose that he earned money on the side. That is not a big fellow. The section provides:
Every person who has
(a)	made, or participated in, assented to or acquiesced in the making of, false or deceptive statements in a return-
Those last words refer to an understatement of income. A return like that would be a deceptive return. I do not care what the source of the income may be. The offence may be a failure to disclose dividends-and some think that failing to disclose them is all right, unless you are caught. If you are, the law will deal with you. It could be that a farmer has understated his returns from the sale of cattle, wheat or what-have-you from his farm, or that a small businessman has understated his sales or overstated his costs, that is, his purchases, has understated his inventories or has two sets of books with regard to receivables. That would be an offence under subsection (1). Subparagraph (b) of subsection (1) provides:
(b)	to evade payment of a tax imposed by this act, destroyed, altered, mutilated, secreted or otherwise disposed of the records or books of account of a taxpayer-
This refers to a man who may have altered his payroll accounts. He might be a small contractor and he might have padded his payroll account in order to inflate his expenses. That is an offence under the act. Or the man may have-
(c)	made, or assented to or acquiesced in the making of, false or deceptive entries, or omitted, or assented to or acquiesced in the omission, to enter a material particular, in records or books of account of a taxpayer-
Of course, he is the taxpayer. Again, the same sort of thing is involved-payroll padding, record falsification, inventory inflation and doing all sorts of other things to your records. Are these offences necessarily the prerogative of the middle-class or the well-to-do? That is what the Minister of National Defence suggested. I suggest to him that the number of prosecutions or threats of prosecution under section 239 will fall more on the smaller categories of taxpayer because they are far more numerous than the well-to-do. The penalty for the offence is a fine of not less than 25 per cent of the tax sought to be evaded and not more than 200 per cent of the amount of that tax. That penalty is imposed on summary conviction plus, if necessary-
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Leblanc) on a point of order.

Yes, Mr. Chairman.

speechtext: The hon. member knows that he does not have to rise on a point of order, but with the permission of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), he may ask him a question.
Agreed, Mr. Chairman.

If the hon. member for Edmonton West is willing to answer my question, I would like to obtain some explanations.
I did not completely understand a while ago, when he pointed out that a 200 per cent penalty was levied and I would like him to repeat his statement, so that I may try to understand how he can arrive at 200 per cent, because section 239(1) reads as follows:
(f) a fine of not less than 25 per cent and not more than double the amount of the tax-
Now, I find it hard to understand how the hon. member can arrive at 200 per cent.

It seems to me that the explanation-

-that the explanation be clear enough. Doubtless, taxes must be paid. The hon. member is aware of this. One must, first, pay the tax. Furthermore, following a summary conviction, a magistrate may impose a fine of at least 25 per cent and at most double the amount of the tax. Double, as I see it, is 200 per cent! One hundred per cent of the tax is the whole tax and double the tax is 200 per cent.
So-

-double the amount of the tax that was sought to be evaded. If the tax that was sought to be evaded was $1,000, the fine could be $2,000. The tax is also recoverable there. In all, the total penalty to the taxpayer would be $3,000. He would have to pay the tax he sought to evade. They would collect that. Then there is a fine of double the amount of the tax, 200 per cent, in addition to which there can be imprisonment of up to two years. However, for all the offences listed under subsection (1) discretion lies with the Attorney General of Canada, because line 3 of page 550 reads:
-at the election of the Attorney General of Canada, be prosecuted upon indictment and, if convicted-
The proof would be the same as it would before a magistrate. However, if a man had altered the books and in the investigation admitted that he had done so, there is no question that he would be found guilty. The evidence will be there. He must then go to jail for at least two months. There is a maximum of five years. If you want to read further, go to section 243, which clearly states:
Notwithstanding the Criminal Code or any other statute or law in force on the 30th day of June, 1948, the court has in any

prosecution or proceeding under this act, no power to impose less than the minimum fine or imprisonment fixed by this act and the court has no power to suspend sentence.
That means there is a mandatory jail sentence; the man has to go to jail. It is that to which I object. There might be a little more consideration of this matter. If it is agreeable, I suggest that we stand this section and go on to others. We are at a bit of an impasse, and we might make some progress on other sections. speechtext: Agreed, Mr. Chairman.

On clause 1-section 241: Communication of Information.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I do not wish to press the committee, but I hope hon. members will find their way through these sections which may have implications.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I wish to ask the parliamentary secretary a question about section 241. It is an interesting section on which we had varying legal decisions some time ago as to the communication of information and the extent to which a criminal or civil court might call upon officials to give evidence. These are just repetitions of sections which are in existence.
In light of those decisions, can the parliamentary secretary give us an indication of the present position in case we want to make alternative suggestions? I admit I have not read recent decisions regarding officials of the department being called upon by the courts to provide information in either criminal or civil cases. We would like to know the facts.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, officials of the Department of National Revenue have absolute privilege in civil cases. With regard to criminal cases there is an exception which is embodied in subsection (3). Other acts have been changed throughout the years to make provision for the kind of evidence that can be called into court. In civil cases, the privilege provided by subsections (1) and (2) of section 241 is absolute. The hon. member will note that in subsection (3) there is an exception that deals with criminal cases and with cases of a criminal nature relating to the administration of this particular act.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It must be related to the Parliament of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It must be related to federal offences, not provincial offences.

I am wondering whether section 241(l)(a) has been related to some of the other acts which are in force. I have in mind especially the new Statistics Canada Act under which powers are granted to certain officials of Statistics Canada to examine income

tax returns in order to compile statistics. There may be other statutes under which similar powers are given-the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act, for instance. The governing words in the bill before us are "except as authorized by this act," meaning the Income Tax Act. There appears to be a very strict limitation on the officials of the Department of National Revenue preventing their communicating any information obtained on behalf of the minister. We read here:
Except as authorized by this section, no official or authorized person shall . .. knowingly communicate or knowingly allow to be communicated to any person any information obtained by or on behalf of the minister for the purposes of this act.
That is a very sweeping restriction designed to secure secrecy of information. Then we come to subsection (2) which provides:
Notwithstanding any other act or law no official or authorized person shall be required to give evidence in connection with any legal proceedings.
That is a limitation. However, subsection (3) says that notwithstanding what is said in subsections (1) and (2) this restriction does not apply in the case of criminal proceedings. A further exception is made in subsection (4). An official or authorized person may communicate information in the course of his duties to other official or authorized persons in connection with the administration or enforcement of the act, that is to say, the Income Tax Act. Then, under subsection (6) provision is made for an appeal from an order of a court requiring an official or authorized person to give evidence, and so on. There is provision for stays of orders, offences are described and penalties proposed for officials of the department who wrongfully disclose information in their possession and, finally, there is a subsection which deals with definitions. Here we find definitions of "officials", "authorized persons," and so forth.
Knowing that the Statistics Canada Act which was dis-cuseed in this session of Parliament includes specific provision for information to be given, I am somewhat surprised that the section does not appear to authorize employees of the ministry of national revenue to communicate this information. There is no doubt that officials of Statistics Canada are allowed access to information from income tax returns and to examine them as a class. This is one exception to the limitations imposed on communication, and there may be others, in which case the section before us may have to be amended. In any case, there are too many "notwithstandings" in it, and even so it may be that the language used is too restrictive to enable the purposes which Parliament has approved to be carried out.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Perhaps I might elaborate on the answer I gave earlier to the hon. member for Peace River and point out that the privilege attached to information here extends even to civil courts. That type of evidence cannot be given in civil appeals concerning income tax assessments, and so on, even though the Minister of National Revenue may be a party to the case. The privilege is absolute in relation to what officials may disclose.
As to the specific point raised by the hon. member for Edmonton West, I think that if all the provisions of subsection (4) were compressed they would read something like this, "An official or authorized person may communi-
December 6, 1971

cate or allow to be communicated information obtained under this act to any person otherwise legally entitled to receive it." The Statistics Canada Act does authorize officials of Statistics Canada to receive for their particular purposes the type of information that is referred to.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Is an authorized person defined in the interpretation section?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The definition appears in the Statistics Canada Act.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Is there a definition in the interpretation subsection relating to section 241?

I think the present language does not cover the situation. For the purposes of clarity it might have been better and more helpful to the lay person, or even for those who are trying to examine this legislation, if it had been spelled out in the bill before us and an authorized person described. There is nothing in the Income Tax Act which tells us clearly who is a person legally entitled to this information.
Is a lawyer who is advising a client obliged to comb all the Statutes of Canada in order to find out who is authorized to get this information? We know that certain people from the Department of Justice would be legally entitled to have access to this information. I would hope the minister might agree to putting a better definition into the Income Tax Act itself. Otherwise we are doing a disservice to the public who must rely on this legislation.
The parliamentary secretary says the information can be given to those who are legally entitled to have access to it. But who are these people? We do not know. It is necessary to look at some other act or at a number of other acts in order to find out. I confess I do not think it is helpful at all.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall section 241 carry?

I wonder whether the parliamentary secretary and the officials would make a distinct note of this so that in due course we might have an amendment to clarify this point, or are we to rely on the jargon of the income tax department or the Income Tax Act in order to enlighten the public?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
We will certainly consider the suggestion. I am not sure it would achieve the simplification of the Income Tax Act which members opposite have been advocating with some considerable force in the past few days, but certainly it is a serious suggestion and we will give it consideration.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall section 244 as amended carry?

Mr. Chairman, I want to reiterate the point made by my colleague from Central Nova that while there are certain procedures under the Criminal Code whereby an individual is protected if there are difficulties in respect of deficiencies in the charges or whatever procedure has been laid out for laying a charge, under the Income Tax Act one can be almost as loose as a goose, to use a trite phrase: however, I believe it puts the point across.
No information or complaint can be called in question for lack of authority of the informant or complainant except by the minister or the one acting on behalf of Her Majesty. In other words, the dice are loaded. If the taxpayer has been charged under an improperly filed information or an incomplete information, that matters not; he cannot challenge it. The only one who can challenge the type of information is the Crown. The taxpayer has the dice loaded against him. Why is it that a taxpayer under these circumstances should be less than a citizen appearing in a criminal court? The parliamentary secretary might like to explain that. Why should a taxpayer be placed in this position?
The taxpayers are the citizens of this country. They are not a group of people who are to be pushed, bullied, plucked, shorn or the subject of slipshod procedures or injustices. We already know that in so much of this act in the past the onus has always been on the taxpayers. A taxpayer had to prove that he was not guilty or that he did not have to pay the tax. Some changes should be made in the administration in this regard. I hope this will be the case.
Just who are the taxpayers of this country? They are the constituents of all hon. members, including the minister and the parliamentary secretary. Yet when it comes to paying income tax, every citizen is supposed to be deemed

December 6, 1971
Income Tax Act
to be something less than a whole individual. Why does that have to be the situation under the Income Tax Act? The stature of the individual is recognized in other statutes and he knows his rights. But under the Income Tax Act his rights are diminished.
What is so holy about income tax that this should be the situation. On whose behalf is this act? Is there something sacrosanct in respect of the government or the Crown or the provinces with regard to income tax vis-a-vis the citizen? Why do they not hold a gun to his head and empty his wallet? Most people feel they do this anyway. Under the Criminal Code, certain standards are applied concerning the rights of the individual. However, when it comes to the Income Tax Act these rights disappear very quickly.
Why should they?

I do not know why. It seems to me there is an entirely wrong philosophy about this. I do not know why the citizen should be any less under the Income Tax Act than he is under the Criminal Code or under any other statutes which establish his responsibility to the state. But in so far as the Income Tax Act is concerned he counts for less than a human being.
Mr. Chairman, I do not often agree with the hon. member for Edmonton West, but I think that some of the things he said tonight reflect my feelings.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member for Edmonton West is usually right.
I did not hear the snide comment of the hon. member for Peace River who is sitting there reading the newspaper in the front row.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. The hon. member said I was reading the newspaper. He knows I never read newspapers in the House, particularly if he is speaking. I was reading my own speech. I find it is a good speech and I wish it had been a little longer.

If so, I withdraw my comments. But I agree with the hon. member for Edmonton West who has pointed out with some force some of the inequities in the penalty provisions of the Income Tax Act, particularly some of the almost vicious and cruel limitations on the judge or magistrate to reduce the fine and to allow a suspended sentence. I can remember cases I fought where rather weak characters appeared in court after having made some bad mistakes as a result of a disaster in the family and who, through desperation, had fallen afoul of the law. The judge had said, "I wish I could give a less severe sentence".
I do not see, as the hon. member for Edmonton West said, why we cannot relax the regulations and give discretion to judges to take the sting out of some of these vicious fines which are often more severe than the fines imposed by vicious loan companies. I think there is much merit in what he said.

Section 244, which is very long, is an important section of the bill and most of it is in the original act. But I think comment should be made about a couple of the subsections. Anyone who has tried to defend a person

charged under the Income Tax Act has found that the procedures under section 244 weigh very heavily in favour of the Crown. The methods of proof are very easy for the Crown but difficult for defence counsel to meet. I do not say that that is necessarily bad. I will point out one particular section on which I would like to have an explanation.
The first few subsections permit the Crown to prove their case against an individual for failure to file, or for a similar offence, by affidavit. Under this section it is sufficient for them to file an affidavit which purports to have been signed by a person who purports to be an official in the minister's office in charge of the records. It has always been difficult for a defendant to prove the negative. The Crown has proven that a notice was mailed out to an individual and that according to the records of the department there was no reply. These two pieces of information added together automatically make the person guilty. Some clerk or secretary in the minister's office signs an affidavit that he is in charge of the records and that according to the records a person was given registered notice on a certain date, but that according to the records there was no response. Under the act that person is guilty of failure to file.
I see that subsection (18) of section 244 seems to give the taxpayer something of a break. I do not have the original act with me, but the note shows that subsection (18) is former section 136 (15) modified. I should like to have it clarified for my own satisfaction in what manner this previous situation has been modified. It seems to me that where formerly the taxpayer was deemed to be guilty, now at least he has a chance of going before a magistrate and saying that he mailed a return and can show a copy of it. The magistrate can then accept the fact that he has filed a return. Yet subsection (18) seems to deal only with proceedings under division J of part I, and I am wondering whether this might raise a defence for the accused person to counteract the heavy onus that is laid on him in the earlier subsections of section 244.
I hope I have made myself clear. I hope that under this amendment the taxpayer will be given a break, and if he is, I think it is a good amendment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The modification to the section about which the hon. member has inquired is a deletion of the reference to division I in the original act. That is the only change to the section.
Therefore my hopes have been dashed and the taxpayer does not get a break.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I should explain to the hon. member that under the revision the old divisions I and J are combined and are found entirely in division J of the bill. So there is no change despite the modification.

I thank the parliamentary secretary for that answer. I had hoped there had been an improvement in the situation. This leaves me with the comment that the procedure set out in section 244 is heavily weighted against the accused person. There are many people who have received notice to file a return. They mail it not by registered mail and then the department claims they never received it. The person claims that he did mail it but
December 6, 1971

it must have gone astray. In many cases this is considered to be a lot of hot air by magistrates, but in some cases magistrates and provincial judges are inclined to accept the excuse. I do not think we can hope for a further amendment on this. So far as I know, judges and magistrates have been reasonable. If a person comes along with any excuse at all, in most cases they hesitate to convict.
I should like to go back for a moment to subsection (4) of section 244 which relates to limitations of prosecutions. There is a five-year limitation under this section, which I think is reasonable. But the part which seems unreasonable to me is the exception, which provides:
An information or complaint. . . may be laid . . . within one year from the day on which evidence, sufficient in the opinion of the minister to justify a prosecution for the offence, came to his knowledge-
It seems to me that according to this provision there is no limitation on the time in which a charge can be laid. I would like to ask the parliamentary secretary if there are any cases in which this section has been used, where prosecutions were brought after five years by reason of certain facts coming to the attention of the minister and, if there are such cases on record, were they anything other than cases considered to be straight fraud?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: While the parliamentary secretary is thinking about that question, on the same section he might answer a point that came to my mind when I read it. Is the knowledge of the officials of the minister deemed to be constructive knowledge of the minister? In other words, let us assume the officials in the department had knowledge which in their opinion justified prosecution but the minister was not acquainted with it. As a lawyer, the parliamentary secretary will realize what I mean.
