speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: GENERAL MOTORS-RECALL OF CERTAIN VEHICLES FOR INSPECTION AND REPLACEMENT OF POSSIBLE DEFECTIVE PARTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was advised late this afternoon, too late for a statement on motions today, with regard to a communication which my office received from General Motors of Canada. I feel it is important that this announcement be made immediately and that it be made in the House.
I want to recommend that all Canadian owners of vehicles involved in the current recall campaign of General Motors of Canada return their vehicles to authorized dealers for inspection and installation of an engine movement restraining device. The notification by General Motors of Canada involves Canadian owners of approximately 600,000 1965 through 1969 regular size Chevrolets and Novas as well as 1967 through 1969 Camaros and certain light trucks, which include some GMC models with similar V8 engines. No Chevelles, Corvettes or six-cylinder models are included in the company's campaign.
I note that General Motors Corporation agreed to initiate this campaign as a result of intensive investigations in the United States and Canada by the company and by officials of the U.S. Department of Transport and of our own ministry of transport. General Motors plans to begin notifying owners by mail as soon as current owners' names can be obtained from Canadian vehicle registration records and as soon as parts can be produced and delivered to dealers.
At very low speeds and heavy throttle, engine-mount failure might result in lifting of the engine and consequent interference with the throttle mechanism. Symptoms of this condition may include momentary sticking of the accelerator pedal, possible transmission shift to neutral, and interference between the engine fan and radiator or fan shroud which would result in a loud noise. Throttle interference could contribute to an accident.
General Motors of Canada have advised me that the engine movement restraining devices should be available at Chevrolet dealerships in the latter part of February. I also note that only in rare instances does engine lift involve the throttle and become a problem following engine-mount separation. I advise that if vehicle operation should be affected by engine-mount separation, the driver should turn off the ignition key and brake the vehicle to a stop. I particularly urge Canadian owners of affected vehicles who have already experienced engine-mount failure to have their vehicles checked and ensure that the restraining devices are installed as soon as available.
I should like to add that I appreciate the co-operation of General Motors in carrying out this program in our country and the fact that they have moved voluntarily.

subsubtopic: GENERAL MOTORS-RECALL OF CERTAIN VEHICLES FOR INSPECTION AND REPLACEMENT OF POSSIBLE DEFECTIVE PARTS
speechtext:
I should like to take the opportunity of thanking the minister for his announcement and his interest. This announcement rein-[The Chairman.]
forces my belief that most large corporations are interested in the welfare of their customers. Had they not been, I submit they would not have become large corporations notwithstanding the continual sniping from certain consumer advocates and advisers. Notifying 600,000 customers by mail has meant a sizeable expenditure for General Motors. In any event, with a view to safety one can take comfort from the fact that the defect is likely to be a minimal cause of accidents.
I commend the minister and the corporation, and heartily endorse the recommendation that customers avail themselves of this service.

subsubtopic: GENERAL MOTORS-RECALL OF CERTAIN VEHICLES FOR INSPECTION AND REPLACEMENT OF POSSIBLE DEFECTIVE PARTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should first like to thank the minister for at least making the statement in the House and not to the press outside the Chamber. I think he is to be commended for that. As we look at the models involved we are speaking about a period from 1965 to 1969. This further points out that we must have a militant and imaginative department to look after the consumer. If we are concerned about consumer protection, we should be moving in the direction of safety regulations.
When you look at the statement made, General Motors is telling us that we have been riding around on a bomb since 1965. I wonder how many cases have come to light where the driver has been charged with responsibility when in fact it was a defect of mechanism. I think it is good that General Motors is recalling these cars. At the same time I would urge the minister to set up strong safety regulations for some type of testing by the department. The consumer in this country is entitled to good protection and this can only be assured through safety regulations. We know that some of our regulations are imported from the United States. We may have added some, but we must take this duty upon ourselves and the government must assure the consumer that safety is a prime concern.

subsubtopic: GENERAL MOTORS-RECALL OF CERTAIN VEHICLES FOR INSPECTION AND REPLACEMENT OF POSSIBLE DEFECTIVE PARTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I be allowed to sincerely congratulate the minister who took the initiative of advising the Canadian people of what General Motors has revealed to him today.
I myself learned this morning the decision of General Motors to recall over 6 million vehicles in North America, over 600,000 of them in Canada. To my mind, this was a gratifying decision because it will protect the consumer to a certain extent.
It will also give this large company the opportunity to check its production methods so that, in the future, it might spare its customers the inconveniences they are now experiencing.
I therefore urge the minister to continue warning people against problems as serious as those the purchasers of General Motors vehicles are now up against.
Adding my voice to that of the minister, I urge Canadians to take advantage of the services offered by General Motors for the correction of the mechanical defects that might crop up.

AIRPORTS-HAWKESBURY-ACTION TO REMOVE POSSIBLE SAFETY HAZARD CREATED BY CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a matter was brought to my attention recently by the Canadian aircraft owners and pilots association which prompted me to question the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) regarding aircraft operation safety at Hawkes-bury airport. As a pilot of some years standing, I am perhaps more receptive to representations from the flying fraternity than those who have never been involved in making decisions from an operator's viewpoint. In this particular instance I feel that the members of a certain flying organization have been dealt with somewhat arbitrarily and I would like to present their side of the case.
The Montreal Soaring Council has operated for more than 15 years out of an airfield located at Hawkesbury, Ontario. This location was chosen, as airports must be, with regard to wind factor, suitable terrain, existing obstructions, etc., all viewed necessarily with safety of the operation as a prime factor. The Hawkesbury location has proved admirable in this respect and over 4,700 flights have already been logged in 1971. With increasing use of the existing licensed runway, expansion is of immediate concern and additional runways have already been planned for construction during 1972 and 1973.
In August of this year the Montreal Soaring Council was approached by officials of the CNR and informed that a spur line of the railway was proposed to cross the southern section of their property, which would have the effect of rendering useless for flying purposes one-third of their airfield. The CNR at this point had already spent considerable time and money on the preliminary stages of the project which was initiated without consultation with the organization owning the property involved. The CNR, as a Crown corporation, does have the authority to take such action under the provisions of the Expropriation Act and the CNR Act. Unlike the CPR, they are not obliged to approach the Canadian Transport Commission prior to construction of a new railway line. When the line is completed, they must then apply to the CTC for an order to operate the line which is by this time completed. But until then no notification of any sort is required. It is not my intention at this time to dispute the provisions of the acts in question but only to point out that inevitably instances arise which might indicate that the authority bestowed by Parliament is being used without proper regard for the rights of individuals and, in this instance, of aviation safety.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
Although prior discussions between the Department of Transport and CNR officials resulted in their agreement that the area of operation remaining after the disposal of the property in question could still be fully licensed under DOT regulations, provision for expansion has not been made, considering the present growth rate of 20 per cent per annum. In addition-this is a most important point and one which is not covered under existing DOT regulations-no separate regulations now exist which govern airfields used by soaring craft as opposed to powered craft. This means that even though an airfield might meet minimum licensing requirements for powered aircraft, those minimum requirements would not necessarily be adequate when applied to soaring craft. There is no indication whatsoever that any consideration was given by the CNR or DOT in their discussions to this most important aspect of the operation.
A glider port such as the Hawkesbury facility must not be compared to an airfield used exclusively by normal power aircraft. For example, a towing aircraft has a slower rate of climb and, with a glider in tow, the angle of take-off must be shallower. The same holds true for landing approaches. There, obstruction clearance limits become more stringent due to the presence of the tow-line dangling behind the tug. Also, since when soaring conditions suddenly wane many sailplanes must land at once, a large operating area is obviously required. Other technical factors are involved. In the interests of brevity I will not list them point by point. I have the material in hand and will be happy to turn it over to the minister or any member of his department who will take the time to peruse it.
The Montreal Soaring Council does not wish to obstruct in any way the task of CNR in building a spur line which has been planned to serve an industrial site a few miles distant and which will prove to be of benefit to property owners and municipalities in the area. The council would be only too willing to co-operate with CNR in selecting a site which would be mutually agreeable to both parties. They would be equally willing to sell CNR such property as would be necessary to construct the line. The Montreal Soaring Council believes that such a site already exists a few hundred feet south of the proposed CNR site. An abandoned Canadian Northern Railway roadbed parallels the highway and the power lines on the southern boundary of the airfield.
Relocation of the rail line to this site, which is a feasible engineering undertaking, would minimize the disruption of the existing facilities of the airfield and allow for future installations to proceed as planned. The spur line could still service those industrial areas, present and future, for which it was intended. It is true that certain sites on the other side of the presently proposed line would not be reached by the route suggested by the Montreal Soaring Council, but that property is owned by the council and it has no intention of selling that particular piece of land for industrial development.
The council feels that the Hawkesbury airfield is a valuable asset to the area. Existing and proposed industries in the immediate vicinity can only benefit from an active, well maintained airfield in the area. A rail line site

is available a short distance from where it has been planned at present. I urge the minister to give earnest consideration to requesting Canadian National Railways to reconsider the route of the spur line and for the company to arrange a meeting with the Montreal Soaring Council in order that the problem may be resolved on a mutually agreeable basis. The Montreal Soaring Council is anxious to co-operate.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gerard Duquet (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
maintopic: AIRPORTS-HAWKESBURY-ACTION TO REMOVE POSSIBLE SAFETY HAZARD CREATED BY CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Pringle) for the opportunity of providing some information to the House respecting the operation of Hawkesbury airport and the effect on its operation of the construction of a spur line by Canadian National Railways. This line will provide access to the Industrial Fasteners Limited wire rod mill at Longueuil, Ontario, and will be approximately 4.44 miles long. The exact location of the line was studied at length by CN before the final one was chosen, and serious consideration was given to alternate routes.
I know of the hon. member's personal interest in the aviation community and all members are, of course, intensely interested in safety. That is why I am pleased to give these assurances with respect to the operation of aircraft at Hawkesbury.

FINANCE-SPECIAL DEVELOPMENT LOAN PROGRAM-SUGGESTED INCREASE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA ALLOCATION-AMENDMENT OF FORMULA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, ever since the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) made his announcement regarding the special loan fund on October 14, I have been critical of the allocation of that $160 million fund as between the various provinces. On November 24 the Minister of Finance sent me a letter setting forth some of the statistics. He wrote: Since the allocation of each provincial share is based largely on its relative share of unemployment, the changes in shares from last year's program to the present program are more readily illustrated by examining the share of unemployment by province. The following table shows the proportion of unemployment in the various provinces to Canada's total for the period June to September, with comparisons with last year.
I ask the House to look at the comparisons. The percentage of the total unemployed in the province of Newfoundland last year was 3 per cent compared to 3.4 per cent this year. The money they will be allocated out of this fund has gone up from $6.8 million to $7.5 million. Prince Edward Island was .4 per cent last year. It is the same this

year. It received $1 million last year and will receive $1 million this year. Nova Scotia had 3.1 per cent of the unemployed last year and 4 per cent this year. Its share of the loan fund has gone up from $4.3 million to $7.4 million. New Brunswick had 3.4 per cent last year and 3.4 per cent this year, exactly the same. However, its allocation has gone up from $5.4 million to $9 million.
Quebec has dropped from 36.6 per cent to 36.3 per cent. Its allocation has dropped from $70.3 million to $63.2 million. Ontario's share of the unemployment went up from 26.1 per cent to 28.8 per cent. Its allocation has gone up from $17 million to $26.5 million. Manitoba went up from 4.1 per cent of the unemployment to 4.4 per cent. Its allocation has gone up from $8.6 million to $9 million.
Saskatchewan was 3.1 per cent last year and 2.5 per cent this year. They did not receive anything last year but will receive $6.9 million this year. Alberta had 5.3 per cent of the unemployment last year. It went down to 5.2 per cent this year. Its allocation went up from $6.8 million to $8.5 million. British Columbia had 14.9 per cent of the unemployed last year. It has dropped this year to 11.6 per cent. Its allocation has dropped from $39.8 million last year to $21 million this year.
There are two extenuating circumstances which the minister pointed out in his letter. British Columbia received $2.8 million of the Saskatchewan funds which Saskatchewan did not use. Even that is $37 million last year compared to $21 million this year. Also, the minister has tabled a formula setting forth the very complicated basis upon which this allocation was resolved. After looking it over I am convinced it has created more anomalies that it has solved.
It is significant that the province of British Columbia, where unemployment in this period this year is a little over 20 per cent less than last year, has had its allocation cut by almost 50 per cent. I am not complaining about what any province is getting. I am simply pointing out that this is a very arbitrary and discriminatory way in which to divide the $160 million between the provinces. I recognize that at this late date the government cannot start to notify the provinces that it has changed the allocation. But what the government could do was what it did last year when it found there were inequities. An additional amount was made available; the government stepped up its original $150 million to $160 million so as to iron out some of the inequities. I urge the government to increase the total amount of the fund so that some of the inequities which are self-evident when one examines the figures I have just quoted may be straightened out and no province is subjected to any sense of discrimination.
Two weeks ago, the province of British Columbia had already used up the entire $21 million despite the fact that neither of the two larger cities, Vancouver and Victoria, had yet made application. My own constituency, one of the municipalities which was very quick to get started on this project, put in proposals for a sewage program but found it was too late and had to take its place on a waiting list. This meant it had to ask the citizens in a referendum to approve going ahead with the sewage project despite the fact that it does not know what the cost will be

because it is not known whether any benefit will be received from the special loan development fund.
I urge the government to seriously consider increasing the amount of the special loan fund above the $160 million at which it is fixed at the present time. I do not know any program which would help to put people to work more rapidly and which would at the same time provide greater social benefits. Should whatever government which is in office repeat the program next year, I hope it will be done six months ahead of time and that a decision to proceed will no longer be left until fall. I would have thought that after the experience of last year, when the announcement came much too late for effective use to be made of the scheme, the government would have acted promptly this year so that measures could be taken by the municipalities to make good use of the funds available.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. D. Alkenbrack (Frontenac-Lennox and Addington):
maintopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-GRANTING OF PAROLE TO NELLES KIDNAPPERS-REFUSAL TO RETURN LICENCE TO PERSON CONVICTED OF IMPAIRED DRIVING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to protest what I believe to be a gross maladministration of justice and a disparate and disproportionate application of the granting of parole by the National Parole Board. On Tuesday, November 23, I put a question to the Solicitor General (Mr. Goyer) as follows:
Can the Solicitor General explain to me and to the House why the parole board is granting parole to the convicted criminal kidnappers in the notorious Nelles case in 1969, after only one-sixth of their sentences have been served, while the same parole board will not grant the return of a driving licence to a penitent constituent of mine?
I am sure Your Honour understands exactly why I raised this question. I suppose I could just as well have directed my inquiry to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner). I do not think it requires a lengthy answer. By asking my question tonight I am simply bringing justice, as it is administered today, into perspective. Canadians are not satisfied with what is going on.
I think the House and the people of Canada deserve an explanation from the Solicitor General, from the Minister of Justice, and especially from the organization known as the National Parole Board. The people of Canada demand to know why Mr. Street and his board have granted parole to most of the gang of criminal kidnappers in the notorious Nelles case after only an average of one-sixth of their sentences have been served. And if Mr. Street and
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
company are to be that lenient with these convicted persons, why can they not be fair and grant a poor youth in my constituency the return of his driving licence which was taken away for two years for a conviction of impairment?
Now, when he and his parents ask for its return, after he has learned his lesson, they are given a terse, curt "no". I point out that it is said that none of the Nelles case men had a previous record. Neither had my constituent who lost his driving licence. He has served well over half of the penalty in being deprived of his driving licence.
Many people do not know that if one is convicted of impaired driving-which is classed as a criminal offence, rightfully-the parole board has, truthfully speaking, the keys of one's car. That is all right. I am not kicking about that, Mr. Speaker. It is perfectly proper that this authority hold that right. But when the parole board uses such disparity and disproportionate judgment as I have just outlined in these two cases it is time the truth was known and it is time it gave reasons for such judgment.
I demand full revelation for the House and the people of Canada of the judgment and record of parole of this high-class gang of criminals in the Nelles case. I demand that the Attorney General smarten up and look into this matter. Or is he pursuing the policy as outlined in his recent statement where he said that this government is more interested in rehabilitation of criminals than in the protection of persons and property?
While I am on the subject, Mr. Speaker, I want to point out to you and the House that according to the Toronto Star of November 27, the man who shot and killed a gasoline filling station attendant, David Seedhouse, last month in Weston, Ontario, had been paroled from prison only last July after serving two years of a six-year term for gas station robberies. The National Parole Board paroled him under these lenient terms, and less than four months later this man committed a brutal murder, shooting down defenceless David Seedhouse who did not have a chance. I want an explanation for these two cases from Mr. Street and his board, and I demand that the Solicitor General sees that the House gets an explanation.
In these times of trouble, especially when one takes into account the terrible circumstances of lawlessness that prevail in our permissive society under this Trudeau government, if a vestige of the hoped for just society is to survive we must pay more attention to the keeping of law and order and to the punishment of criminals and transgressors in a manner consistent with the sentences that the courts of justice are handing down. Is there any justice in sentencing a man who makes a practice of robbing service stations at gunpoint to a deserved six years and then having the parole board let him out in two years to pave the way for him to commit capital murder four months later? The answer the Canadian people give to that question is an unequivocal "No."
That is why I say I am bringing justice into perspective here tonight when I say to the Attorney General for God's sake, if he is going to allow the paroling of all the Nelles gang, in the name of justice return to my young constituent his driving privileges. If we can get this done, I will give the parole board my constituent's name. I do not mention it here tonight as a matter of courtesy because I

do not wish to embarrass him and his family. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that my request this evening will receive an early and favourable response from the Attorney General and his department. I remind him that the people of Canada are awaiting an explanation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas A. Hogarth (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-GRANTING OF PAROLE TO NELLES KIDNAPPERS-REFUSAL TO RETURN LICENCE TO PERSON CONVICTED OF IMPAIRED DRIVING
speechtext:
As the hon. member knows, individual decisions pertaining to the granting of parole are made by the National Parole Board. This applies to all persons in custody of the federal government. As the hon. member further knows, the parole board is a quasi judicial body vested with certain powers under the Parole Act, and the whole concept of granting these powers to a board is based upon the premise that such matters should not be the subject of political interference, political influence or political decision. Accordingly, in so far as such decisions are concerned, the Solicitor General (Mr. Goyer) even though he may from time to time, as the hon. member has done here tonight, question an individual case, he is not only reluctant to interfere but indeed he cannot.
Explanations as to why parole is given in any one individual case would take much more than the three minutes that I have. The files are elaborate and the reasons are equally elaborate. In any event, it is impossible and not in the interest of justice, I suggest, to balance one case against another. There is no reason, because a kidnapper is paroled in Toronto, for a young man in the hon. member's constituency to have his driver's licence reinstated, nor is there any reason, because the young man
should not have his driver's licence reinstated, for the kidnappers in Toronto to be kept in jail. There is no correlation between the two cases. Careful consideration must be given to each case.
The Solicitor General is quite satisfied that although from time to time apparent errors are made, such as would appear in the case of the filling station attendant who was shot, nonetheless the parole board has given careful consideration in each instance. The Solicitor General is prepared to admit that parole is a very difficult matter. In modern penology, where the risks are between the protection of the public and the rehabilitation of an individual, those risks are equal. The parole board will, hopefully, come down in favour of the individual, giving him the benefit of the doubt as being a rehabilitated citizen. Sometimes this does not always work but it is found that in most cases it does, and although the hon. member has suggested a few failures there are many thousands of successes that go unheralded and unheard of in this great country.
I direct the hon. member's consideration to an article that appeared in the Vancouver Sun last Saturday dealing directly with this point. In any event, if the hon. member wishes to have his views further known, on December 15 the Senate judicial committee is commencing an inquiry into parole policy and the parole board, as well as how the Solicitor General's functions relate to this board. He is certainly welcome to appear there and to present such views as he has presented this evening.
